INDUSTRY
If you're taking the time to read this book and
learn about prototyping games, it's probably
safe to assume that you might have some
interest in joining the game industry.
In this chapter I present a little information
about the current state of the industry
and then talk a bit about university games
education programs. I give you some tips on
meeting people, networking, and looking for
work. Finally, I tell you about how to prepare
for your own projects.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
288 CHAPTER 15 the dIGItal Game IndUstry
About the Game Industry
The most definitive thing that I can tell you about the game industry right now is that it
continues to change. When I wrote the first edition of this book, Riot Games had spent
the last half-decade growing from a tiny start-up in 2008 to one of the largest game
companies in Los Angeles. Over the decade since the first edition, they have continued
to expand League of Legends and have started selling a few other games, but they have
also had significant issues with sexism within their company, a reckoning that was long
overdue and has swept across many studios in the industry.
A lot of big names such as Electronic Arts and Activision are still around, as they have
been for the last three decades; however, they have stayed in the industry by shifting
the kinds of games that they are making. It wasn't too long ago that no one would have
believed a cell phone could be one of the most successful game platforms, but sales of
games for mobile devices (phones and tablets) are now worth over $85 billion per year.
1
As you read this, the specific market numbers are probably different, but in this chapter,
I show you trends over time and point you to resources where you can find the most
recent numbers.
Entertainment Software Association Essential
Facts
The ESA (http://theesa.com) is the trade association and lobbying organization for most
large game development companies, and it was the ESA who argued before the United
States Supreme Court for games to be protected by the first amendment. The ESA
releases a yearly report on the state of the game industry called the "Essential Facts"
that you can find by searching for "ESA essential facts" on the Internet.
2
Certainly the
reports have some bias issues (the ESA's job is to see the game industry through rose-
colored glasses), but the reports are still a good way to get an idea of what the overall
industry looks like. Here are some key takeaways from the Essential Facts 2021 report on
the gaming market in the United States:
3
1. In the United States, 67% of adults (age 18+) and 76% of kids play games,
for a total of 226.6 million players in across all ages in the U.S. (up from
214.4 million in 2020), with the average player being 31 years of age.

3. 55% of gamers said that they played more during the COVID-19
pandemic of 2020–21, and 70% of parents said that they allowed their children
to play more games during the pandemic. The biggest change in play habits during
the pandemic was that 77% of players said that they played with others (online or
in-person) at least weekly (up from 65% in 2020, which is an increase from
139 million in 2020 to 174 million in 2021).
4. Across all players, casual games dominated, with 63% of players regularly enjoy-
ing casual games (this number increases to 71% on PC and smartphones but is less
on consoles). Several popular genres of games were regularly enjoyed by 30–40%
of players, including action games (39%) such as Super Mario Oddysey, shooter
games (39%) such as Fortnite, racing games (37%) such as Forza, family games
(33%) such as Just Dance, and adventure games (31%) such as Uncharted.
5. E (Everyone) continues to be the most popular rating for games, with 49% of all
games rated E (Everyone). 16% of games were E10+ (Everyone 10+), 21%
were T (Teen), and only 14% were M (Mature).
6. Another major change due to the pandemic was that 74% of parents now report
playing games with their children at least weekly (up from 55% in the 2020
report), with 57% of parents saying that games are fun for all of them, and 53% say-
ing video games are a great way for the family to spend time together.
7. The vast majority of parents also have specific household rules about their children's
gaming: 90% require children to get their permission before spending
real money in a game, 83% require their children to get their permission
before playing any game, 78% have rules about the amount of screen
time, and 77% say their children must have their permission before
communicating with others online.
Conditions in the Industry
A lot has changed since the first edition of this book, and in that time, some major
trends have emerged.
The Industry Continues to Grow
The ESA Essential Facts documents contained data about sales in the digital game
industry from 1996 to 2017.

The ESA estimates that content spend grew from $3.7 billion in 1996 to $29.1 billion in

throughout the 2008 financial crisis and that the increase in spending accelerated con-

platforms (which also happened in 2008). In fact, in a 2021 document, Accenture esti-

There Are Gamers of All Genders and Ages
In many of their Essential Facts documents, the ESA pointed out that in the United
States, women over 30 are a larger portion of the gaming audience than men under 18.

Though the way the ESA sliced and published age and gender data changed from year-
to-year, I've done my best to represent it in Figure 15.2.
In the graphs of Figure 15.2, the numbers in each colored column section represent the
youngest age in that demographic section. For example, you can see in the top graph
that in 2002, 45% of gamers were under 18 (green), 36% were between 18 and 35 (yel-
low), and 19% were 36 or older (red). Contrast that with 2021, when 20% of gamers
were <18, 38% were 18–34, 14% were 35–44, 12% were 45–54, 9% were 55–64, and 9%
were 65 or older. As you can see, the ESA used different age groupings over the years,
but the trend of gamers under 18 shrinking from 45% of the market to only 20% and the
trend of gamers 35 or older growing from 19% to 42% represent a massive shift. In gen-
eral, the percentage of adult gamers has grown drastically over the past two decades.
Figure 15.2 ESA's United States gamer audience breakdown by age from 2002–2021 8

Generating the actual data I'm charting took a lot of massaging of the data to get useful
information, because the ESA—as an industry lobbying group—is very selective in choosing
the data that they will present and how it is presented. The worst omission was that the total
gaming audience in the United States was only reported for 2002, 2015, and 2019–21, so I
interpolated the total in the unreported years. However, I do believe that the general trends
represented are correct.

Whereas the top graph of Figure 15.2 shows the full hundred percent of gamers in every
column, the bottom graph reveals that the total number of gamers in the United States
grew from 145 million in 2002 to 226.6 million in 2021. So, even though the percentage
of under-18 gamers shrank from 45% to 20% (a relative drop of 56%), the actual number
of gamers under 18 went from 65.3 million to 45.3 million (only a 30% relative drop).
On the other hand, the number of gamers over 35 went from 27.6 million to 95.2 million,
which is a 244% increase!
Figure 15.3 ESA's United States gamer audience breakdown by gender from 2002–2021 9
Figure 15.3 shows the total number of game players in the United States identifying as
women and men (to the closest million). In 2002, for example, there were 55 million
female gamers and 90 million male gamers (totaling 145 million). Over the past two
decades, the number of players in the U.S. who identify as women has grown from

57862.content:
55 million (38%) in 2002 to 102 million (45%) in 2021, while the total number of gamers
identifying as men has grown from 90 million in 2002 to 125 million in 2021. There have
always been a very high number of women gamers, despite the fact that the majority of
game advertisements have targeted men. Accenture also found that worldwide, women
account for 60% of new gamers (gamers who have played for four years or fewer)! In
the Accenture document, 48% of gamers identified as women, 52% identified as men,
and 2% identified as non-binary or chose to not answer. With Accenture's estimate of
2.7 billion gamers worldwide, that's roughly 54 million gamers out there who chose to
not identify as male or female, yet very few games that have human characters include
non-binary characters.
Working Conditions at Game Companies
If you know nothing about the game industry, you might think that working at a game
company is fun and easy. If you know a little about it, you might have heard that game
9. Ibid.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
aBoUt the Game IndUstry 293
company employees routinely work 60-hour weeks with mandatory overtime for no
additional pay. Though the real story now for most companies is better than that, the
stories you might have heard were based on fact, and I do have friends in the industry
who still sometimes have mandatory 70-hour workweeks (10 hours/day, no weekends)
during "crunch time" on their projects, but luckily that trend has diminished greatly
over the past two decades. Now, most companies, especially larger companies, will still
sometimes ask you to work overtime, but the stories of game developers who haven't
seen their partners or kids for a week have become rarer (though sadly, they do still
exist). However, before starting to work at any company, you should make sure you
understand their overtime compensation policy and history of crunch time on projects.
Rising Costs of AAA Development
Each generation of gaming consoles has seen a rise in the cost of developing a top title
(also known as a AAA game, which is pronounced "triple-a"). Teams for AAA titles are
now routinely more than 100 or 200 people, and even some with apparently small
teams actually have outsourced several aspects of the game's development to other stu-
dios with hundreds of their own employees. It is now typical for a AAA game budget to
exceed $100 million and have a combined total team of more than 1,000 people spread
across several studios.
The effect of all of this on the game industry has been the same as the effect that
budget inflation had on the film industry: The more money that a company spends on
a project, the less willing it is to take risks. This is why in Figure 15.4, of the top 20 best-
selling games of 2020, only four games are not sequels.

The Rise of Freemium Games
According to Flurry Analytics, during a six-month period between January and June of
2011, free-to-play games rapidly overtook paid games in terms of iOS revenue.
12
In Janu-
ary of 2011, premium games (which are purchased upfront) accounted for 61% of the
game revenue on the iOS App Store. By June, that number had crashed down to 35%,
with 65% of revenue then coming from freemium games (also called free-to-play games),
where the player gets the game for free but is asked to pay small amounts to gain game-
play advantages or customization. The percentage of freemium games is even greater
now, and the freemium model catapulted Zynga from a six-person start-up in 2007 to
more than 2,000 employees in just a few years. However, this model has been shown to
work much better for casual games than more traditional genres, and some developers
of more traditional genres who are now creating mobile games have chosen to return
to the premium model because they believe that their market is averse to the freemium
model.
A few freemium games have done well with a more core (i.e., less casual) audience of
gamers. The primary differentiating factor between these and the casual freemium
games is that many of the casual games allow and encourage players to purchase a
competitive edge in the game (i.e., pay more to win more), whereas core games like
Team Fortress 2 (TF2) only allow players to purchase aesthetic items (e.g., hats) or items
that change game mechanics without making them imbalanced (e.g., the Black Box
rocket launcher for Soldiers that has a 25% smaller clip size (3 instead of 4 rockets) yet
can grant the Soldier +20 health whenever it hits an enemy). In addition, nearly every
item that is purchasable in TF2 can alternatively be crafted by players from items gained
through gameplay. The critical element in this is that core players don't want to feel that
someone else has bought a gameplay advantage over them.
The largest non-casual freemium game is currently Fortnite, by Epic Games, which is

available for free on nearly all platforms. Money is made in Fortnite by encouraging
players to purchase season passes that allow them to earn cosmetics and other items
through play (players without the season pass do not earn items through play). Because
players spend the full amount on the season pass whether or not they actually earn the
items, they are incentivized to play (in order to "get their money's worth"), which keeps
the number of concurrent players in Fortnite very high, something that is necessary for
the Fortnite battle royale game style to work.
12. "Free-to-play Revenue Overtakes Premium Revenue in the App Store" by Jeferson Valadares
(July 7, 2011), http://web.archive.org/web/20140108025130/http://blog.flurry.com/

July 26, 2021.

aBoUt the Game IndUstry 295
Whether you choose to go for freemium or premium relies largely on the genre of
game you want to develop and the market and type of players that you are seeking.
There are several other models out there, including ad-supported games and games
that sell "seasons" of additional gameplay or narrative as downloadable content (DLC).
Look at other games in the market and see what the standards are, then decide whether
you want to go along with them or buck the trend.
Games as a Service
In 2017, Microsoft created Game Pass, which was followed by Apple Arcade in 2019.
Each of these are gaming services in the same way that Netflix is a video service. Not
only do these each provide access to more than 100 games for a relatively low monthly
fee, Apple Arcade actively funds development of new games. Just like Netflix and Ama-
zon Prime have funded a wide breadth of different video content, Apple has funded a
wide breadth of independent game content, providing money to found several small
studios and showcase new dev talent. This up-front investment allows the studios to
create premium-style games without relying on players to purchase the game before
playing it. As I'm writing this, Netflix has just announced that it is also planning a game
service. There have also been some strong moves toward streaming gaming services
where the actual game runs on a computer in a server farm and streams to the player's
television over the Internet (the most famous of these was Google Stadia), but as of
2021, none of them have gained large market share yet.
The Continued Development of the Indie Scene
While AAA games have become much more expensive to create, the ubiquity of free or
cheap game development tools like Unity, GameMaker, and Unreal Engine has led to the
rise of a worldwide independent development community to an extent that has never

57865.content:
been seen before. As you'll see when you read the rest of this book, almost anyone
can learn to program, and dozens of developers have now proven that all you need to
make a game is a great idea, some talent, and a lot of time. Many of the most famous
independent game projects started as the passion project of a single person, including
Minecraft, Spelunky, and The Stanley Parable. IndieCade is a game conference that started
in 2005 and is dedicated exclusively to independent games.
13
Beyond that, dozens of
other conferences either focus on independent development or have a track or contest
for indie developers, and the rise in digital delivery has provided small developers a
much easier way to market and sell their games. Of course, there is a lot of competition
out there, but making video games is now easier than it has ever been, and the rest of
this book can teach you how.
13. Full disclosure: Since 2013, I have been the IndieCade Chair of Education and Advancement
and have programmed the IndieXchange (2013–21) and Game U (2013–15) aspects of the
conference. I'm honored to be part of such a fantastic organization and conference.

296 CHAPTER 15 the dIGItal Game IndUstry
Game Education
Over the past two decades, game design and development education at the university
level has gone from a curiosity to a legitimate field of study. The Princeton Review now
ranks the top graduate and undergraduate game programs yearly, and some programs
even offer Ph.D. degrees in games and game studies.
People generally have two core questions about these programs:
■ Should I enroll in a game education program?
■ Which game education program should I choose?
Should I Enroll in a Game Education Program?
As a professor who has spent more than a decade teaching in these programs, I can
say that my answer to this question is a qualified yes. Game education programs offer
several clear benefits:
■ You have a concentrated space and time in which to build your design and
development skills in a structured way.
■ You'll be surrounded both by faculty who can give you honest, meaningful feedback
on your work and peers who can become great collaborators. In addition, many of
the faculty in these programs have worked in the game industry and have connec-
tions to several game companies.
■ Many game companies actively recruit from the top schools. Being at one of them
means that you could have the chance to interview for an internship with one of
your favorite studios.
■ When new employees are hired out of university game programs—especially
master-level programs—they usually enter the company at a higher level than others.
Traditionally, people got into game companies by working in QA (quality assurance)

57866.sourceSearchName: introductiontogamedesignprototypinganddevelopment3e introductionto game design prototyping and development from concept to playable game with unity and c
57866.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57866.heading: INDUSTRY
57866.content:
and testing games. If they excelled at QA, they could get noticed and move up into
one of the other positions. Although this is still a very valid way to enter the industry,
I have seen new people coming out of university programs often get hired above
talented people with several years of seniority who came up through QA.
■ Higher education in general will push you to grow and become a better person.
However, you should be aware of some caveats. School takes both time and money. If
you don't have a bachelor's degree, I personally think that you should absolutely get
one. Throughout your life, it will open more doors and grant you more opportunities
than not having one. A master's degree is much less necessary in the industry, but
programs at the master level are able to offer much more focused education and can
be truly transformative. Master's programs generally take between two and three years
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
Game edUCatIon 297
and can cost $60,000 or more. However, as my professor Dr. Randy Pausch was fond
of saying, your time should be more of a consideration for you than the cost of educa-
tion. Long-term debt and predatory lending practices are real concerns and have raised
the potential price of an advanced degree. But even with that being the case, the most
important question you should ask yourself is whether getting an advanced degree
is worth two to six years of your life when you could potentially have been out in the
industry already. When I chose to go to graduate school for game development, it was
because I wanted to change the trajectory of my career (from programming to game
design and teaching). I chose to spend two years of my life paying money instead of
earning it, and for me, that decision absolutely paid off. You must do what you feel is
right, of course.
Which Game Education Program Should I
Choose?
Hundreds of universities now offer game education programs, and new ones are
being added every year. The Princeton Review's list of the top schools is generally well
respected, but picking a school that is right for you and what you want to do with your
career is much more important. Take time to research the program and learn about the
classes and faculty. Investigate how much emphasis the program puts on the different
aspects of game development: design, art, programming, management, and so on. Do
the program's faculty currently work in the game industry, or do they focus entirely on
teaching? Each school will have certain aspects that are their strengths.
Entertainment Technology Center — Carnegie Mellon University
As a student, I attended Carnegie Mellon University's Entertainment Technology Center
(ETC) for my Master of Entertainment Technology degree. At its core, the ETC is based

around teamwork and client work. In the first semester (which was for me the best
educational semester I have ever experienced), each incoming student works on five
collaborative two-week assignments with a randomly selected team of peers in a class
called Building Virtual Worlds (BVW). The incoming class size is generally more than
60 students, and this helps them experience working with new people continuously
throughout the semester. In that semester, each person works about 80 hours each
week
14
on their team assignment in addition to taking two or three other classes that
supplement BVW. Then, for the remaining three semesters, each student is assigned to
a single project team for the full semester and takes only one additional class. Most of
these semester-long projects have a real client for whom they are being produced, so
ETC students learn firsthand how to manage client expectations, work with peers, and

handle internal disputes. These projects are designed to give students several years'
worth of industry experience in only two years of grad school. The goal of the ETC is
to prep game designers, producers, programmers, and technical artists for work on
industry teams.
Interactive Media & Games Division — Univ. of Southern California
In contrast, the Master of Fine Arts program in the Interactive Media & Games Divi-
sion (IMGD) at the University of Southern California (where I taught for four years) is
structured very differently. The size of the incoming cohort each year is now generally
30 students, and they all take several classes together in the first year. Though there are
group projects, the students do several independent assignments as well. In the second
year, students are encouraged to branch out and explore their personal interests. Stu-
dents take roughly half of the classes in the second year with their cohort, but they can
select the other half of the classes from across the university. The third year in the IMGD
is devoted almost entirely to each student's work on their individual thesis project.
Though each student leads a thesis project, students very rarely work alone. Most thesis
teams are 6 to 10 people in size, and the other team members are pulled from interested
students across the university. Each thesis project also has a thesis committee composed
of mentors from the industry and academia who are interested in the project and led by

57868.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57868.heading: INDUSTRY
57868.content:
a thesis chair from the IMGD faculty. The stated goal of the IMGD is to create thought
leaders, and as such, it is more important to this program that the individual students
grow and produce something innovative than that they are prepared for industry jobs.
USC has been ranked #1 by the Princeton Review in either the undergraduate or gradu-
ate level every year since the rankings began.
Media and Information Department — Michigan State University
In my current job, I teach Game Design and Development students in the Media and
Information Department at Michigan State University, which, in 2021, was ranked the
#1 undergraduate game program at a public university.
15
In addition to a major, we also
have a highly selective interdisciplinary minor program that is the reason for our high
ranking. Our minor focuses on prepping students to go directly into professional jobs
in the industry. One of the major advantages of the program being a minor is that every
student in the program gets major-level experience in Games and Interactive Media,
Computer Science, or Studio Art (the three most common majors in the game develop-
ment minor) as well as the best possible game design and development education avail-
able at our university. This is very different from most other universities where the minor
students get a second-class version of games education.
15. MSU's game program was ranked the #1 program at a public university (#7 overall) as
reported by the Princeton Review, https://www.princetonreview.com/press/game-
design-press-release-2021. Read more at https://comartsci.msu.edu/about/newsroom/news/
gamedev-msu-ranks-1st-us-public-university-programs-game-design — both accessed
July 30, 2021.

There Are Many Other Schools Out There
As you can imagine, each of these programs benefits students in very different ways.
I have chosen these three to illustrate the point because they are the three with which
I am most familiar, but every school is different, and you owe it to yourself to learn the
goals that each school has for its students and how it hopes to achieve them through
the classes it teaches.
The number of schools offering game development classes is ever increasing, with
more than 500 universities now offering game programs. Nearly all undergraduate and
graduate schools recommended by the Princeton Review have a lot to offer. I can also
personally vouch for the excellence of both DigiPen and the University of Utah's Enter-
tainment Arts & Engineering program.
Several trade schools also teach game development, including the online school
Gnomon (https://www.gnomon.edu/). These trade schools can be good if you know
exactly what you want, but make sure that you know their reputation. While Gnomon is

excellent, many game development programs at trade schools (and some universities)
are not worth your time or money. The most important thing is to do your research and
make sure you know what you're getting into.
Getting Into the Industry
I have condensed the content in this section from the "Networking with the Pros" talk
that I gave at the 2010 Game Developers Conference Online. If you would like to see the
expanded version, you can find the slides on the website for this book.
16
Meeting People in the Industry
The best way to meet people in the game industry is to go where they are. If you're
interested in board games, this means Gen Con; if you are interested in AAA develop-
ment, this means the Game Developers Conference in San Francisco; and if you're
interested in independent game development, this means IndieCade. Many other
conferences out there are quite good, but those are the three that have the biggest draw
from each of those groups.

17. E3 and PAX are also famous game conferences, but E3 is a marketing conference, and
PAX is primarily a fandom conference, so you're less likely to interact with actual game
developers there. Some very cool smaller conferences include the Game Devs of Color
Expo ( https://www.gamedevsofcolorexpo.com/ ), Foundations of Digital Games ( http://
foundationsofdigitalgames.org/ ), DiGRA ( http://www.digra.org/ ), PAX Dev ( https://
dev.paxsite.com/ ), and MSU's Meaningful Play ( https://www.meaningfulplay.msu.edu/ ) —
sites all accessed July 30, 2021.

300 CHAPTER 15 the dIGItal Game IndUstry
However, being at a dev conference only means that you are co-located with game
developers. To meet them, you must find a way to go up and say hello. Some good
times to do so include parties, after a talk that they've given, and when they're work-
ing their company's booth or publicly demonstrating their game. However, in each of
these cases, you need to be courteous, concise, and respectful both to the developer
and especially to the other people who want to talk to them. Game developers are
busy people, and they each have a reason to be at the conference. They, too, want to
meet people, expand their networks, and talk shop with other developers. So don't
take too much of their time, don't ever make them feel trapped in a conversation with
you, and always have something to bring to the table. That is, make sure that you have
something to say that will be interesting to them before you start the conversation. One
good approach to "something to say" is to compliment something specific about their
game and then ask a question that demonstrates you're thinking about the game as a
designer/developer, not just a fan.
Speaking of fans, when meeting famous people for the first time, don't fawn over them.
Every game designer from Will Wright to Jenova Chen is a regular person, and very few
of them have any interest in being idolized. Along these lines, avoid saying things like
"I love you! I'm your biggest fan!" Frankly, that's pretty darn creepy. Instead, it's much
better to say something like, "I really enjoyed playing Journey." That way, you're compli-
menting the game—a game that several people worked on—rather than complimenting
the individual person, about whom you actually know very little. Also, this is not the
time to ask for a job; instead you should exchange business cards and ask whether you
can contact them later.
Of course, the very best time to meet someone new is when you're introduced. This
gives you an in as well as something to talk about (your mutual friend). However, when
this happens, you have a critical responsibility to the friend who introduced you—the

responsibility to not make them look bad. Whenever someone introduces you, they are
vouching for you, and if you do something embarrassing, it reflects badly on them.
Also, don't just focus on meeting famous game developers. Everyone at these confer-
ences loves games, and students and volunteers at the conference are some of the most
passionate and creative people you can talk to. Plus, who knows—anyone you meet at
a dev conference could be the next great designer everyone is talking about, and later
they'll be a great friend to have take a look at your games as you develop them.

57872.heading: THINGS TO TAKE TO ANY GAME CONFERENCE
57872.content:
THINGS TO TAKE TO ANY GAME CONFERENCE
If you're going to meet people, you should always have business cards on you.
You can put whatever you want on the front, as long as you make sure it's leg-
ible. I usually recommend leaving the back largely blank so that the person to
whom you give the card can write notes on it that will remind them later of what
you talked about. Honestly, you don't need to spend a lot on these cards, just get
good, non-glossy paper with decent printing, and you'll be fine.
Other things I tend to take with me include the following:
■ ■ Breath mints and toothpicks: Seriously.
■ ■ A pocket tool such as a small Leatherman: Being the person in the
room who can fix little things that break is nice.
■ ■ A résumé: I don't carry these with me anymore because I'm very happy
with my current job, but if you're seeking a job, you really want to have a
few copies with you.
■ ■ A mobile version of your portfolio or game: Someone might ask to
see some of your work, and the most unobtrusive way to do so is to have
it on your phone or tablet. If your game doesn't run on a mobile device,
you can take a laptop with you, but even then, a better way is to first
show a short video on your phone and then invite them to play on your
laptop if they're really interested.
Following Up
So, you've met someone at the conference and gotten their business card. What's the
next step?
About two weeks after the conference, write the person an email. You generally want to
wait a couple of weeks because everyone is completely flooded with emails and work
when they get back from a dev conference. Your email should generally follow a format
similar to that shown in Figure 15.5.
Send the letter and wait a couple of weeks. If you don't hear anything back, write one
more time with a lead in like "I'm willing to bet that you were pretty busy after the con-
ference, so I wanted to write again and make sure that you got my email."

Interviewing
If everything goes well, you might have a chance to interview at the studio. Now, how
do you prepare?
Questions to Ask Before the Day of the Interview

57873.sourceSearchName: introductiontogamedesignprototypinganddevelopment3e introductionto game design prototyping and development from concept to playable game with unity and c
57873.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57873.heading: THINGS TO TAKE TO ANY GAME CONFERENCE
57873.content:
When you interview, you'll be talking to people who are actually on game development
teams. Before the interview, the person you talk to will usually be a recruiter. Part of
the recruiter's job is to make sure that candidates are properly prepared for the inter-
view, and their evaluation at the end of the year will be partially based on the quality of
candidates they brought in. This means that it is in a recruiter's best interest for you to
be perfect for the job, and they are more than willing to answer any questions that can
help you better prepare for the interview.
Questions to ask include the following:
■ What would my job be? You want to know the answer to this as specifically as
possible so that you can prep.
■ On which project would I be working? This also answers whether the com-
pany is interviewing you for a specific position or is interested in hiring good people
regardless of what project they will work on.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
GettInG Into the IndUstry 303
■ What is the company culture like? Each company culture is different, particular-
ly in the game industry. A question like this can also lead to a discussion of things like
overtime and crunch time. You don't really need to know the answer to questions
about company culture before interviewing, but you definitely need to know them
before you sign a contract.
■ What would be appropriate for me to wear to the interview? Many, many
people skip this simple but important question. In general, I tend to dress more for-
mally than I would on a normal workday, but for most game companies, that doesn't
mean wearing a suit (and it almost never means wearing a tie). Remember, you're not
going to a nice dinner, a party, a date, or a religious ceremony. My wife, a professional
costume designer and professor, recommends this: You want to look nice, but you
want to make sure that the focus is on your skills and mind, not on how you look.
Another thing to consider is that though you definitely want to wear something
that makes you feel comfortable, you also want to wear something that makes the
interviewers feel comfortable. Every studio talks at some point to investors, the press,
publishers, and other people who tend to work in more formal cultures than a game
development studio. One of the things that the studio needs to know about you is
whether you can be part of those discussions or whether they would have to hide
you in a back room so you don't embarrass them when guests visit. Be sure that they
place you in the former category.
There are a lot of different opinions out there on the web about what is appropriate
to wear, so the best thing you can do is ask the recruiter. The recruiter will have seen
every candidate who comes in, and they'll know what works and what doesn't.

57874.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57874.heading: THINGS TO TAKE TO ANY GAME CONFERENCE
57874.content:
In addition to clothing, you should also think about making sure your hair (including
facial hair, if you have any) looks deliberate instead of accidental.
■ Are there any games by other studios that I should play before the
interview? You absolutely must play games made by the studio where you're
interviewing before you go in, and if you're interviewing to work on a specific game,
not having played it or its prequels is unforgivable. This question helps you under-
stand which other games they think you should have played to be knowledgeable
about the state of the art in their genre.
■ Should I expect a test as part of the interview? Many jobs might have a
design, programming, or art test for you to take. Sometimes they'll give this to you
to take home and work on prior to the interview, and sometimes (particularly in the
case of programming tests), they'll want you to work through it with them. As with
most things in an interview, if you don't know something, it's okay to say so. Several
programmers I know use the test to ask the potential employee an extremely difficult
or unusual problem to see how they think through something challenging and new.
■ Can you tell me who will be interviewing me? If you know this ahead of time,
you can do some research into their background. Knowing other projects that your
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
304 CHAPTER 15 the dIGItal Game IndUstry
interviewers worked on before coming to the current studio or other studios where
they worked previously can give you more insight into their background and more
things to talk about.
Some questions you should definitely not ask include the following:
■ What games has the studio made? / How long has the studio been
around? The answers to these questions are easily available online. Asking something
like this makes it seem like you haven't done your research before coming to the inter-
view (and consequently like you don't really care much about the interview or job).
■ How much will I get paid? Though this will eventually be a very important ques-
tion, asking this of an interviewer or recruiter is inappropriate. Instead, it will be part
of your negotiations after you have been offered the job. For information on industry
averages, you can look to the Video Game Developer Salary information at Game
Industry Career Guide
18
or sites like glassdoor.com.
■ Any specific technical questions. The recruiter generally won't know much
about the specifics of development technology at the company, so it's best to save
those questions for the interview.
During the Interview
Myriad resources are available on interviewing well, so I'll just give you a few thoughts
here. Be yourself, be curious, and be willing to let them know when you don't know

57875.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57875.heading: THINGS TO TAKE TO ANY GAME CONFERENCE
57875.content:
the answer to something they ask. Pay attention to body language and try to learn
what you can about the culture of the company. Remember that you're also interview-
ing them and you want to make sure that their company is the right fit for you. Most
interviewers will give you some time to ask your own questions of them, so make sure
that you have something to ask that demonstrates that you are serious about the job. If
possible, I also tend to take notes throughout the day so that I can remember specific
things that I discussed with each person.
After the Interview
After the interview, one of the best things you can do is to send handwritten thank you
notes to the people with whom you spoke. This is where those notes that you took can
really help you. "Thank you very much for walking me through the studio and especially
for introducing me to Team X" is much better than "It was great to meet you, and I'm
glad we talked about generic things." Just like items in games, handwritten letters are
valuable because they are rare. Every month, I get thousands of emails, more than 100

an excellent magazine that ceased publication in 2013. There isn't a new source that is as
definitive, but the content at Game Industry Career Guide seems pretty good. https://
www.gameindustrycareerguide.com/video-game-developer-salary/ — accessed July 20, 2021.

printed letters through postal mail, and less than 1 handwritten thank you note. Hand-
written notes are never spam.
Don't Wait to Start Making Games!
Just because you're not yet a game company employee doesn't mean that you can't
make games. After you've finished this book and gotten some experience programming
and developing prototypes, you'll probably be looking for a game to work on. Here are
some tips for that time.
Join a Project
I'm sure you have a ton of great ideas for games bouncing around in your head, but the
best thing you can do if you're new to development is to join a team that already has
some experience developing a game. Working with a team of other developers—even if
they're still learning like you are—is one of the best ways to quickly grow your skills.
Start Your Own Project
After you've either gotten some experience on a team or if you just can't find a team to
work with, it's time to start creating your own games. To do so, you need six critical
elements: the right idea, the right scope, the right team, the right schedule, the right
ways to communicate, and the will to finish.
The Right Idea
Millions of different game ideas are out there. You need to pick one that will actually
work. It must be something that you know will continue to interest you throughout the

57876.sourceSearchName: introductiontogamedesignprototypinganddevelopment3e introductionto game design prototyping and development from concept to playable game with unity and c
57876.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57876.heading: THINGS TO TAKE TO ANY GAME CONFERENCE
57876.content:
project, something that doesn't just copy a game you love, something that other people
find interesting, and most importantly, something that you know you can make. This
leads us to…
The Right Scope
The number one thing that stops teams from finishing games is overscoping —in other
words, biting off more than you can chew. Most new developers don't understand
how long making a game can take, so their game concepts are drastically overscoped.
Scoping-down is the process of getting the game down to its bare essentials and elimi-
nating fluff. For a game to have good scope, you must have a true and realistic under-
standing of the amount of effort needed to implement the game, and you must make
sure—you must be absolutely certain—that you have the team and the time to finish it.
Making a tiny game and expanding on it is drastically better than starting by trying to
make something huge. Remember that most games you have played took a large team
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
306 CHAPTER 15 the dIGItal Game IndUstry
of professionals about two years and millions of dollars to make. Even indie games often
take years of work by an experienced and talented team. When you're just starting out,
think small. You can always add more to the game later, and a series of small, finished
games is one of the best ways to both build your skills and your portfolio. See Chapter 7,
"Acting Like a Designer," for more information on project scope.
The Right Team
Working on a game with someone is a long-term relationship, and you need to treat it
that way. It's also sadly true that the things that make you great friends with someone
might not be the same things that are required to make you great team members. When
you're thinking about working with people, make sure that they have similar work
habits to yours, and it's best if they tend to work at similar times of day as well. Even if
you're part of a remote team, texting or video chatting with your teammates while you
work can really help.
While creating your team, you also need to have a conversation about ownership of
the intellectual property (IP) of the game. If no agreement is in place, the default is that
everyone who had anything to do with the project owns an equal share.
19
IP issues are
sticky, and they might seem kind of ridiculous to talk about before any game exists, but
it is a critical conversation to have. However, the flip side of this is that I have actually
seen game teams never get started because people were bickering about the IP owner-
ship of a game that didn't exist. You definitely don't want to get stuck in that trap.

57877.heading: ROYALTY POINTS
57877.content:
ROYALTY POINTS
At my company, I've been using royalty points as what I believe to be a fair way of
distributing royalties for work done on the independent games we make. The core
idea of royalty points is that everyone earns royalties for time that they dedicate to
the project throughout the entire development of the project. Here's how it works
for my teams:
■ Half of any income for a project goes directly to the company. This helps
us build up cash so that we can pay people in the future (right now,
people are working exclusively for future royalties).
■ The other half is distributed to people who worked on the project based
on their percentage of the total royalty points.
19. I am not a lawyer, and I am not trying to give legal advice. I'm just sharing my personal
understanding of the situation. If you have a friend who is a lawyer, I recommend asking
them about it or looking for information online.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
don't waIt to start makInG Games! 307
■ For every 10 hours of work that someone puts in to the project, they earn
1 royalty point. I chose this number because it's about one week of part-
time work.
■ These points accrue throughout both the development and support of
the project.
■ The points are tracked in a spreadsheet that any member of the team can
view at any time (though only I can edit it).
With this royalty point system, team members directly earn royalties as they work
on the project, and the more good work they do, the larger percentage of the roy-
alties they will earn. If someone on the team isn't doing good work, you remove
them from the team, and they still earn royalties for the work they did do, but they
earn a smaller and smaller percentage relative to the other team members who
are continuing to contribute.
This also means that members of the support or live ops (i.e., live operations) team
could eventually have a greater percentage of the royalty points than the original
development team; this is by design. Most small, independent projects in the past
have granted a specific percentage of royalties to each person at the beginning
of the project, which makes it very difficult to alter things in the future and adapt
to a changing work situation. I believe that royalty points allow you flexibility as
a studio while still being clear and fair to everyone involved. If you're interested
in an even more egalitarian structure for your entire business, you could look into
making your company a worker cooperative, a company that is owned and man-
aged democratically by its workers.
20
20. For more information on worker co-ops in game development, check out this article about
a panel discussion at the Game Devs of Color Expo ( https://www.gamedevsofcolorexpo.

57878.content:
com/ ) by Alex A.K. (creative director at Soft Not Weak), Francesca Esquenazi (co-founder,
CEO and producer at Future Club), and Eva-Léa Longue (secretary and animator at Lucid
Tales): https://www.gamesindustry.biz/articles/2021-10-06-an-introduction-to-game-worker-
cooperatives – links accessed October 23, 2021.
The Right Schedule
In Chapter 14, "The Agile Mentality," I cover Agile development practices and burn-
down charts. Make sure that you read it before you start a project. Though your mileage
may vary, I have found that for my teams and the vast majority of my student teams,
burndown charts are a fantastic tool to keep us on track and aware of where each per-
son is in their individual development tasks. In addition, burndown charts do a fantastic
job of helping you to understand the difference between how long you estimate a task
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
308 CHAPTER 15 the dIGItal Game IndUstry
will take and how long it actually takes you to accomplish it. By looking at the difference
between the two in the chart up to the point where you are currently, you can get a
more realistic estimate of how long completing the remaining tasks will take.
The Right Ways to Communicate
One thing that the COVID-19 pandemic taught us is that we can't always expect to be
working in the same location with the rest of our teams. If you're going to be working
with a remote team, spend a good amount of time at the beginning making sure that
you have a communication structure that works for everyone. For most of my student
teams in 2021, that has meant a combination of Discord and the burndown chart from
the previous chapter. However, technology will continue to evolve. Also make sure that
your team is all on the same page in terms of not only communication technology but
also the right times to communicate; if you have both morning people and night owls
on your team, you need to know when to reach out to whom.
The Will to Finish
As you make progress on your project, you will come to a point where you clearly see
all the things that you could have done better. You'll see that your code is a mess, your
art could be better, and the design has some holes in it. A lot of teams get to this point
surprisingly close to the end of the project. If you are near the end, you need to push
on through. You must have the will to finish your game. If the number one killer of games
is bad scoping, the number two killer is that the last 10 percent of the project is always
the hardest climb. Keep pushing, because even if the game isn't perfect—and trust me,
no game ever is —even if the game isn't all you hoped, even if it is far less than what you
hoped, it will be done. You will be a game developer with a finished title, and that means

57879.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57879.heading: ROYALTY POINTS
57879.content:
a tremendous amount to everyone you hope to work with in the future.
Summary
There is much more to be learned about the game industry than was able to fit in this
single chapter. Luckily, many websites and publications cover the game industry, and
talks at conferences often address both what it takes to join the industry and the process
of starting a company. A simple web search should surface several of them, and the
GDC Vault (http://gdcvault.com) is a great place to find videos of many talks.
If you do choose to start a company, be sure that you find a lawyer and an accountant
that you can trust to help you before you actually run into any bumps in the process.
Lawyers and accountants have years of training in how to build and protect companies,
and having them available to consult can make your path to incorporation much easier.

SYSTEMS
If you've never programmed before, this chapter
will be your introduction to a new world: one
where you have the ability and skills to make
digital prototypes of the games you imagine.
This chapter describes the mindset you need
to have when approaching programming
projects. It gives you exercises to explore
that mindset and helps you think about the
world in terms of systems of interconnected
relationships and meaning.
At the conclusion of this chapter, you will be in
the right mindset to explore the challenges of
the subsequent chapters in Part II of this book.

312 chapter 16 Thinking in Digi T al Sy ST em S
Systems Thinking in Board Games
In the first part of the book, you learned that games are created from interconnected
systems. In games, these systems are encoded into the rules of the game and into the
players themselves, meaning that all players bring certain expectations, abilities, knowl-
edge, and social norms to the games that they play. For example, when you think about
a standard pair of six-sided dice as used in many board games, the dice carry specific
expected and unexpected behaviors with them:
■ Common expected behaviors of 2d6 (two six-sided dice) in board games
1. Each die is rolled to generate a random number between 1 and 6 (inclusive).
2. The dice are often rolled together, especially if they are the same color and size.
3. When rolled together, the dice are usually summed. For example, a 3 on one die
and a 4 on the other would sum to a total of 7.
4. Rolling "doubles" (that is, both dice roll the same value) sometimes grants a
special benefit to the player (e.g., in Monopoly, doubles allow a player to roll
again).
■ Common unexpected behaviors of 2d6 in board games
1. A player will not just place the dice on the values that they would prefer to have.
2. The dice must stay on the table and must land completely flat on a side to be
considered a valid roll. Otherwise, they are rerolled.
3. After the dice are rolled, they are generally not touched for the rest of that
player's turn.
4. Dice are generally not thrown at other players (or eaten).
While it may seem somewhat pedantic to explore such simple, often unwritten, rules in
detail, it serves to show how many of the rules of board games are not actually present
in the rule book; rather they are based on the shared understanding of fair play among
the players. This idea is incumbent in the concept of the magic circle,
1
and it's a large
part of what makes it so easy for a group of children to spontaneously create a game
that they all intuitively understand how to play. Most human players carry within them
massive preconceptions about how games are played.
Computer games, however, rely on extremely specific instructions to do absolutely

everything. At their core—regardless of how powerful they have become over the past
several decades—computers are mindless machines that follow very simple instructions
several million times per second. It is up to you, the programmer, to provide the
computer with a semblance of intelligence by encoding your ideas into simple, pedantic
instructions for it to follow.

on the magic circle.

An Exercise in Simple Instructions
One classic exercise for budding computer science students to help them understand
how to think in terms of very simple instructions involves telling another person how to
stand up from a prone position. You'll need a friend for this.
Ask your friend to lie on their back on the floor, and after they are there, ask them to
please only follow your exact instructions to the letter. Your goal is to give your friend
instructions that will move them into a standing position. However, you cannot use
any complex commands like "stand up." Instead, you must only use the kind of simple
commands that you might imagine giving to a robot. For example:
■ Bend your left elbow closed 90 degrees.
■ Extend your right leg halfway.
■ Place your left hand on the ground with your palm facing downward.
■ Point your right arm at the television.
In reality, even these instructions are drastically more complex than anything that could
be sent to most robots, and they're pretty open to interpretation. However, for the sake
of this exercise, this level of simplicity will suffice.
Give it a try. Don't worry; I'll wait.
How long did it take you to give your friend the right instructions to stand up? If you
and your friend try to follow both the rules and the spirit of the exercise, it will take
quite a while. If you try it with different people, you'll find that it takes much, much
longer if your friend doesn't know ahead of time that you have the end goal of getting
them into a standing position.
How old were you the first time you were asked by a member of your family to set the
table for a meal? I think I was only about four when my parents decided that I could
handle that complex task with my only instruction being, "Please set the table for din-
ner." Based on the exercise that you just completed, imagine how many simple instruc-
tions you would have to give to a robot to recreate the complex task of setting the table,
yet children are often able to do this before they start elementary school.
What This Means to Digital Programming
Now, of course, I didn't give you that exercise to discourage you. In fact, the following
two chapters are meant to be really inspirational! Rather, it was given to help you under-

for aspects of computer programming. Let's take a look.

314 chapter 16 Thinking in Digi T al Sy ST em S
Computer Language
When I gave you the list of four example commands that you could give, I was outlining
the parameters of the language that you could use to talk to your friend. Obviously, this
was a pretty loose language definition. Throughout this book, we will be using the pro-
gramming language C# (pronounced "see sharp"), and thankfully, its language defini-
tion is far more specific. Later in this part of the book, we'll explore C# much more, but
suffice to say that I have taught thousands of students several different programming
languages over more than two decades, and my experience has shown me that C# is
one of the best languages for someone to learn as their first programming language.
Though it requires slightly more diligence than simpler languages like Processing or
JavaScript, it gives learners a far better understanding of core development concepts
that will help them throughout their game prototyping and development careers, and it
enforces good coding practices that will eventually make your code development faster
and easier.
Code Libraries
In the previous exercise, you can see that it would have been much easier to have been
able to tell your friend to "stand up" rather than going through the trouble of having to
give so many low-level commands. In that case, "stand up" would have been a multi-
purpose high-level instruction that could be used to tell your friend what you wanted
regardless of the starting position that they were in. Similarly, "please set the table" is a
common, high-level instruction that generates the desired outcome regardless of what
meal is being prepared, how many people will be eating, or even what household you
are in; and it can adapt to any cultural context. In C#, collections of high-level instruc-
tions for common behaviors are called code libraries, and hundreds of them are available
to you as a C# and Unity developer.
The most common code library that you will use is the collection of code that tailors C#
to work properly with the Unity development environment. In your code, this extremely
powerful library will be imported under the name UnityEngine. The UnityEngine
library includes code for the following:
■ Awesome lighting effects such as fog and reflections
■ Physics simulations that cover gravity, collisions, and even cloth simulation
■ Input from mouse, keyboard, gamepad, and touch-based tablets
■ Thousands of other things
In addition, thousands of free (and paid) code libraries are available to help make your
coding easier. If the thing you want to do is pretty common (e.g., moving an object

The prevalence of great code libraries for Unity and C# means that you can concentrate
on writing code for the new, unique aspects of your games rather than reinventing
the wheel every time you start a new game project. In time, you will also start
collecting commonly used bits of your own code into libraries that you will use across
multiple projects. In this book, we will start doing so by creating a code library called
ProtoTools that will grow in capability across several projects in this book.
Development Environment
The Unity game development environment is an essential part of your development
experience. The Unity application can best be thought of as an environment in which
to collect and compose all the assets that you create for a game. In Unity, you will bring
together 3D models, music and audio clips, 2D graphics and textures, and finally the
C# scripts that you author. None of these assets are created directly within Unity; rather,
through Unity they are all composed together into a cohesive computer game. You will
also use Unity to position game objects in three-dimensional space, handle user input,
set up a virtual camera in your scene, and finally compile all of these assets together
into a working, executable game. The capabilities of Unity are discussed extensively in

Breaking Down Complex Problems into Simpler Ones
One of the key things you must have noticed in the exercise is that the exclusion from
giving complex commands like "stand up" meant that you needed to think about
breaking complex commands down into smaller, more discrete commands. Although
this activity was difficult in the exercise, in your programming, you will find the skill
of breaking complex tasks into simpler ones to be one of the greatest tools that you
have for tackling the challenges that you face and helping you make the games you
want one small piece at a time. This is a skill that I use every day in my teaching and the
development of my games, and I promise that it will serve you well. As an example, let's
break down the Apple Picker game that you will make in Chapter 29, "Prototype 1: Apple
Picker," into simple commands.

Game Analysis: Apple Picker
Apple Picker is the first prototype that you will make in this book (built in Chapter 29,
" Apple Picker "). It is based on the gameplay of the classic Activision game Kaboom!,
which was designed by Larry Kaplan and was published by Activision in 1981.
3
Many
clones of Kaboom! have been made through the years, and ours is a somewhat less
violent version. In the original game, the player moved buckets back and forth in an
attempt to catch bombs being dropped by a "Mad Bomber." In our version, the player
uses a basket to collect apples that are falling from a tree (see Figure 16.1).
In this analysis, we will look at each of the GameObjects
4
in Apple Picker, analyze each of
their behaviors, and break those behaviors down to simple commands in flowchart form.
This will demonstrate how simple commands can lead to complex behavior and fun
gameplay. I recommend searching for "play Kaboom!" online to see whether you can
find an online version of the game to play before digging into this analysis, but the game
is simple enough that doing so is not necessary. You can also find a version of the Apple
Picker game prototype on the http://book.prototools.net website under Chapter 16 or
find it in the iOS or Android stores. It's worth noting that our Apple Picker game is only a
single endless level, whereas Kaboom! had eight different difficulty levels.
Figure 16.1 The Apple Picker game you will make in Chapter 29

Apple Picker Basic Gameplay
The player controls the three baskets at the bottom of the screen and is able to move
them left and right using the mouse. The apple tree moves back and forth rapidly while
dropping apples, and the player must catch the apples in the baskets before they fall
past the bottom of the screen. For each apple that the player catches, they earn points.
If a single apple falls off screen, it and all other remaining apples will disappear, and
the player will lose a basket. When the player loses all three baskets, the game is over.
(There are a few other rules in the original Kaboom! game about the number of points
earned per bomb (apple) and how the various levels progress, but those are unimport-
ant for this analysis.)
Apple Picker GameObjects
In Unity terminology, any object in the game—usually meaning anything that you
see on screen—is a GameObject. We can also use this term in discussing the elements
in the screenshot shown in Figure 16.2. For later consistency with our Unity projects,
I capitalize the name of all GameObjects (e.g., Apples, Baskets, and AppleTree) in the
following list.
Figure 16.2 Apple Picker with GameObjects labeled
a. Baskets: Controlled by the player, the Baskets move left and right following the
player's mouse movements. When a Basket hits an Apple, the Apple is caught,
and the player gains points.
B. Apples: The Apples are dropped by the AppleTree and fall straight down. If an
Apple collides with any of the three Baskets, it is caught and disappears from the
screen (granting the player some points). If an Apple passes off the bottom of
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
318 chapter 16 Thinking in Digi T al Sy ST em S
the screen, it disappears, and it causes all other Apples on screen to disappear
as well. This ends the current round and destroys one of the Baskets (starting at
the bottom). When this is resolved, the next round begins, and the AppleTree
starts dropping Apples again.
c. AppleTree: The AppleTree moves left and right randomly while dropping
Apples. The Apples are dropped at a regular interval, so the only randomness in
the behavior is the left and right movement.
In the version of Apple Picker that you'll code later in the book, the player will be limited
to three baskets, and therefore limited to three rounds of play. However, for the sake of
simplicity in this example, we'll just focus on a single round.

Apple Picker GameObject Action Lists
In this analysis, we're not going to consider the difficulty levels and round structure that
are present in the original Kaboom! game. Instead we will focus on the moment-
to-moment actions taken by each GameObject.
Basket Actions
Basket actions include the following:
■ Move left and right following the player's mouse.
■ If any Basket collides with an Apple, catch the Apple.
5
That's it! The Baskets are very simple.
Apple Actions
Apple actions include the following:
■ Fall down.
■ If an Apple passes the bottom of the screen, the round ends.
The Apples are also very simple.
AppleTree Actions
AppleTree actions include the following:
■ Move left and right randomly.
■ Drop an Apple every 0.5 seconds.
The AppleTree is pretty simple, too.

Apple Picker GameObject Flowcharts
A flowchart is often a good way to think about how the flow of actions and decisions
works in your game. Let's look at some for Apple Picker. Though the following flowcharts
refer to things such as adding points and ending the round, right now, we're just look-
ing at the actions that take place in a single round, so we're not worrying about how
those kinds of scoring and round actions actually work.
Basket Flowchart
In Figure 16.3 the behavior of the Basket has been outlined in a flowchart. The game
loops through this flowchart every frame (which is at least 30 times every second). This
is shown by the oval that is at the top left of the chart. Actions are shown in boxes (e.g.,
Match Left/Right Mouse Movement), and decisions are shown as diamonds. See the side-
bar "Frames in Computer Games" to learn more about what constitutes a frame.

57890.content:
FRAMES IN COMPUTER GAMES
The term frame comes from the world of film. Historically, films were composed of
strips of celluloid containing thousands of individual pictures (known as frames).
When those pictures were shown in quick succession (at either 16 or 24 frames per
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
320 chapter 16 Thinking in Digi T al Sy ST em S
Apple Flowchart
The Apple has a pretty simple flowchart as well (see Figure 16.4).
Figure 16.4 Apple flowchart
second (fps)), it produced the illusion of movement. Later, on televisions, themove-
ment was constructed from a series of electronic images projected onto the screen,
which were also called frames (and operated at about 30 fps in the United States).
When computer graphics became fast enough to show animation and other
moving images, each individual image shown on the computer screen was also
called a frame. In addition, all the computation that takes place leading up to
showing that image on screen is also part of that frame. When Unity runs a game
at 60 fps, it is not only displaying a different image on screen 60 times per second;
in that time, it is also calculating the tremendous amount of math required to
properly move objects between one frame to the next.
Figure 16.3 shows a flowchart of all the computation that would go into moving
the Basket from one frame to the next.

AppleTree Flowchart
The AppleTree flowchart is slightly more complex (see Figure 16.5) because the
AppleTree has two decisions to make each frame:
■ Does it change direction?
■ Does it drop an Apple?
The decision of whether to change direction could just as easily come before or after the
actual movement. For the purposes of this chapter, either would have worked.

Summary
As you've now seen, digital games can be broken down into a set of very simple
decisions and commands. This process is implicit in how I approached creating the
prototypes for this book, and it is something that you will do yourself when you
approach your own game design and development projects.
In Part III of this book, Chapter 29, " Apple Picker," expands upon this analysis and shows
how to convert these action lists into lines of code that make your Baskets move, your
Apples fall, and your AppleTrees move around like a Mad Bomber dropping…Apples.

throughout the rest of this book and the Unity Hub: a tool to manage both your Unity

Downloading Unity
First things first, let's start downloading Unity. The Unity installer is more than 1 GB in
size, so depending on your Internet speed, this could take anywhere from a few minutes
to a couple of hours. After you've gotten this process started, we can move on to talking
about Unity.
note
UNITY CHANGES THEIR WEBSITE FREQUENTLY These instructions were
accurate at the end of 2021, but they may not be exactly accurate by the
time you're reading this chapter. If these instructions don't work, you can
also try http://unity.com/download or just explore their website. Unity wants
you to download their game engine, and you should always be able to find
a free option, even if it isn't by following these instructions.
If the process changes drastically from what is listed here, I will post
updated instructions to this book's website, http://book.prototools.net,
under Chapter 17.
Downloading and Installing Unity Hub
The first thing you'll need to do is download the Unity Hub. Unity Hub is a small appli-
cation that manages your Unity installs and projects, allowing you to install multiple
versions of Unity (which I've found very useful while writing this book) and to have one
place to go to open any of your projects. After you've installed Unity Hub, then you can
use it to install the correct version of Unity.
1. Go to http://unity.com, which is, of course, another great place to learn more about
Unity.
2. Click the Get started button in the header bar at the top of the window.
You should be taken to the Unity Plans and pricing page, which has several paid options
that you do not want right now.
3. Click the Student and hobbyist tab. This takes you to at least one free option that you
do want. Both have eligibility information below them.
The Personal license is open to almost anyone, whereas the Unity Student license
requires you to be enrolled in an accredited educational institution. If you are a student,
I recommend eventually getting the Student license, because it grants you five seats
of Unity Teams Advanced (rather than the three seats of Unity Teams Basic granted by
the Personal license). Those extra two seats and access to Unity Cloud Build can be a

You will probably encounter a Windows Security Alert telling you that it has blocked

Installing Unity 2020.3 LTS
Now that you have Unity Hub installed and running, it's time to install the latest LTS
(Long-Term Support) version of Unity 2020.3. The LTS versions are guaranteed by
Unity to have locked functionality and to be supported for at least two years beyond
their original release date. Unity 2020.3 LTS will be supported with monthly update
releases until at least March 2023, all of which will improve performance and stability,
and none of which will change any of the functionality. If when you're reading this, it is
after March 2023, you will still be able to download Unity 2020.3 LTS, and at that time,
it will benefit from over two years of stability improvements and bug fixes, so every-
thing in this book will still work very well.

57899.content:
VISUAL STUDIO ALTERNATIVES
Several very good Integrated Development Environment (IDE) options are avail-
able for Unity C# programming (listed here in my personal order of preference):
■ Visual Studio for Mac (VSMac) is installed automatically with Unity
on macOS, and it is shown throughout this book. I have sometimes had
problems with VSMac getting bloated and slower over weeks of using it,
which have led me to look at alternatives, but it's still my first choice on
macOS. https://visualstudio.microsoft.com/vs/mac/
■ Visual Studio Community (VSComm) is installed automatically
with Unity on Windows, and it is also shown in this book. Some Win-
dows users have also reported slow performance due to all the bloat in
VSComm, but it's still my top choice for Windows. https://visualstudio.
microsoft.com/vs/community/
■ Visual Studio Code (VSCode) is an open source C# development envi-
ronment for macOS and Windows that is maintained by Microsoft but is
much lighter-weight and performant than VSComm. You must install a
few free tools to get it to work well with Unity, but after you have, it's a
very good alternative. There are hundreds of free plug-ins, and I've used
it for both C# and JavaScript coding. If you want to use something other
than VSMac or VSComm—especially if you have an older computer—this
is my recommendation. http://code.visualstudio.com

■ JetBrains Rider is the professional development environment that I've
used while writing this book.
1
JetBrains initially wrote tools to make Visual
Studio better and then created its own IDE that is very robust and very
configurable. Rider is not higher on this list because its keyboard com-
mands are more convoluted than VS options (at least on macOS) and
because it is pretty expensive. However, if you are a student or educator,
you can get a free license. https://www.jetbrains.com/rider/
■ Visual Studio Professional and Enterprise are paid versions of
Microsoft's professional coding environment. If you're a professional
programmer or a computer science student, you may already have
this installed on your machine. It should work fine, but it might not be

■ MonoDevelop was the default C# development environment installed
with Unity for many years, but Unity switched to Visual Studio around 2016.
I haven't used MonoDevelop much since then. http://monodevelop.com
Why Choose Unity?
There are many game development engines out there, but I focus on Unity for several
reasons:
■ Unity is free: With the free Personal version of Unity, you can create and sell games
that run on a multitude of platforms. As of the writing of this edition of the book,

in Unity Personal. There are limitations on who is eligible to download the free Per-

also now offers several individual services and enhancements to Unity that make it
easier to use for professional developers (like Unity Teams Advanced, Cloud Build,
and Build Server) that you could pay for, but you do not need any of them for the

possible like Visual Studio C# code.
