UNITY PRICING Though they have always offered a free option, Unity has
made several changes to its licensing and pricing structure since the first edi-
tion of the book was written, so I recommend exploring the current pricing
at http://store.unity.com.
■ Write once, deploy anywhere: The free version of Unity can build applications
for macOS, PC, the Internet via WebGL, Linux, iOS, Apple tvOS, Android, Samsung TV,
Tizen, and Windows Store—all from the same code and files. This kind of flexibility is at
the core of Unity; in fact, it's what the product and company are named for. Profes-
sionals can even use Unity to create games for the Nintendo Switch, PlayStation 5,
Xbox Series X/S, and several other game consoles.
■ Great support: In addition to excellent documentation, Unity has an incredibly
active and supportive development community. Millions of developers use Unity,
and many of them contribute to the discussions on Unity forums across the web. The
official Unity forum is at https://forum.unity.com/.
■ It's awesome!: My students and I have joked that Unity has a "make awesome"
button. Although this is not strictly true, there are several phenomenal features built
in to Unity that will make your games both play and look better by simply checking
an option box or adding a component. Unity engineers have already handled a lot of
the difficult game programming tasks for you. Collision detection, physics simula-
tion, pathfinding, particle systems, draw call batching, shaders, the game loop, and
many other tough coding issues are all included. All you need to do is make a game
that takes advantage of them!
Why Choose C#?
For many years, Unity offered the choice of three possible languages (C#, JavaScript, or
Boo). Then there were just two (C# or JavaScript), and since then, C# has emerged as the

57901.sourceSearchName: introductiontogamedesignprototypinganddevelopment3e introductionto game design prototyping and development from concept to playable game with unity and c
57901.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57901.heading: VISUAL STUDIO ALTERNATIVES
57901.content:
only coding option for Unity, and that is for several good reasons.
C# was initially developed in 2000 as Microsoft's response to the Java language that was
developed by Sun Microsystems in 1995. C# took a lot of the modern coding features
of Java and put them into a syntax that was much more familiar to and comfortable
for traditional C++ developers. This means that C# has all the capabilities of a modern
language. For you experienced programmers, these features include function virtual-
ization and delegates, dynamic binding, operator overloading, lambda expressions,
and the powerful Language INtegrated Query (LINQ) query language, among many
others. For those of you who are new to programming, all you really need to know is
that working in C# from the beginning will make you a better programmer and proto-
typer in the long run. Over the four years that I taught the game programming class at
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
IntrodUCInG oUr develoPment envIronment 331
the University of Southern California, I initially taught JavaScript before transitioning to
C#, and I found that students who were taught C# consistently produced better game
prototypes, exhibited stronger coding practices, and felt more confident about their
programming abilities than their peers who had been taught JavaScript in prior semes-
ters of the class. Additionally, with Unity's new Data-Oriented Tech Stack, if you really
need speed and are willing to accept some limitations on how you write your code, the
Unity Burst Compiler can compile C# to machine language that is even faster and more
efficient than is possible with C++.
On the Daunting Nature of Learning a Language
There's no way around it: Learning a new language is tough. I'm sure that is one of the
reasons that you bought this book rather than just trying to tackle things on your own.
Just like Spanish, Japanese, Mandarin, French, or any other human language, some
things in C# won't make any sense at first, and there are places that I'm going to tell you
to write something that you don't immediately understand. There will also probably
be a point where you are just starting to understand some things about the language
but feel utterly confused by the language as a whole (which is the exact same feeling
you would have if you took one semester of Spanish class and then tried to watch soap
operas on Telemundo). This feeling comes for almost all of my students about halfway
through the semester, and by the end of the semester, every one of them feels much
more confident and comfortable with both C# and game prototyping.
pro tip
90% OF BUGS ARE JUST TYPOS. I've spent so much time helping stu-
dents fix bugs that now I can very quickly spot a typo in code. The most
common include the following:

57902.heading: VISUAL STUDIO ALTERNATIVES
57902.content:
■ Misspellings: If you type even one letter wrong, the computer
won't have any idea what you're talking about.
■ Capitalization: To your C# compiler, A and a are two completely
different letters, so variable, Variable, and variAble are all
completely different words.
■ Missing semicolons: Just like almost every sentence in English
should end in a period, nearly every statement in C# should end
in a semicolon (;). Leaving the semicolon out often causes an error
on the next line. FYI: C# and many other languages use a semicolon
because the period is already used for decimal numbers (e.g., 3.141)
and what's called dot syntax in variable referencing (e.g.,
varName.subVarName.subSubVarName).

Rest assured, this book is here for you, and if you read it in its entirety, you will emerge
with not only a working understanding of C# but also several simple game prototypes
that you can use as foundations on which to build your own projects. The approach
that I take in this book comes from many semesters of experience teaching "nonpro-
grammers" how to find the hidden coder within themselves and, more broadly, how
to convert their game ideas into working prototypes. (Though some of the following
information appears in the Introduction at the beginning of the book, I'm elaborating
more here.)
Part III—Game Prototype Tutorials
Each tutorial in Part III of this book is composed of three steps:
1. Concept introduction: Before asking you to code anything for each project, I'll tell
you what we're doing and why. This general concept of what you're working toward
in each tutorial gives you a framework on which to hang the various coding elements
that I introduce in the chapter.
2. Guided tutorial: I guide you step by step through a tutorial that demonstrates
these concepts in the form of a playable game. Unlike with some other approaches, I
have you compile and test the game throughout the process so that you can identify
and repair bugs (problems in the code) as you go, rather than trying to fix all of
them at the end. Additionally, I'll even guide you to create some bugs so that you
can see the errors they cause and become familiar with them; this will make it easier
to deal with encountering your own bugs later.
3. Repeat and expand: In many tutorials, I ask you to repeat something. For in-
stance, in Chapter 31, "Space SHMUP—Part 1," a top-down shooter game like
Galaga, the tutorial guides you through the process of making one single enemy
type, and then in Chapter 32, "Space SHMUP—Part 2," you create four others. Don't
skip this part! This repetition can really drive the concept home and help your under-
standing solidify later. Several of the tutorials are broken into two chapters:

57903.content:
■ Part 1: The first half of a two-part tutorial is just about getting the game work-
ing at all. The end result is what you could call an early prototype—the first time
that you can actually play the game in any meaningful way.
■ Part 2: The second half of these two-part tutorials gets them to the point that
many devs call the "first playable"—the first version of the game that is really
playable by someone outside your dev team. The second half adds many more
elements such as additional enemies, more polished movement, or a Graphical
User Interface (GUI) that shows the score, player health, etc. These are still pro-
totypes and nowhere near a polished game, but they have more elements that
make them actually feel like a game and are ready to be taken into playtesting to
get feedback from others.

Earlier, I mentioned that most of my students feel confused and daunted by C# at about
the midway point of the semester, and it's at exactly that time that I assign them Coding
Challenges like those in Part IV of the book.
Part IV—Next Steps
Part IV of the book is dedicated to helping you make the transition from following tutori-
als in this book to creating your own games.

Chapter 37—Coding Challenges
The Coding Challenges chapter introduces you to a type of project that you can find on
the book's website. One of my favorites is Updraft, a simple glider game challenge that
I developed in 2020.
2
In a Coding Challenge like Updraft, you will be presented with a
starter project and some—but not all—of the code for a simple game. This often includes
all the named functions with parameters specified but with only comments (instead of
code) inside the function, describing what you need to write. The key concept here is to
transition your thought process from "I'm following this tutorial" to "I want to do this—
now how do I make it happen?" Coding Challenges are something completely new to
the third edition of the book, and I'm very excited to be giving them to you. I tend to
develop a new challenge each semester and will continue to build the library of them
on the website for this book, under Chapter 37.
Going Beyond…
After you've completed a few of the Coding Challenges, I encourage you to try what I
call a Classic Game Project. When I assign this to my students, they are asked to faithfully
recreate the mechanics and game feel of a classic game over the course of four weeks.
Some great examples have included Metroid, Castlevania, MegaMan, and even Crazy
Taxi. By being forced to work things out on their own, to schedule their own time, and
to dig deeply into the inner workings of these seemingly simple games, the students
come to realize that they understand much more C# than they thought, and that is the
time that everything really falls into place. Another key element of the Classic Game
Project is that you can figure out how to code the game without having to figure out the
design of the game at the same time. At the end of this book, you will be prepared to
tackle your own game projects (or your own Classic Game Project, if you want). Addi-
tionally, the tutorials and challenges in this book can be a fantastic starting point on
which to build your own games. For further information on continuing to improve your
game development practice after finishing this book, check out Chapter 38, "Beyond
This Book."
2. Huge thanks to my former teaching assistant Ellie Locatis, who in 2018 first proposed the
concept of these challenges as simple game projects to help prepare students to start
developing their own code.

I spent well over 1,000 hours writing the third edition of this book and working
extremely hard to make my code as clean and readable as possible. When you first start

57905.content:
creating your own C# scripts, the code you come up with is not going to be that clean,
and there's no reason you should expect it to be. One of the core tenets of how I teach
game prototyping is: as long as the game runs, the code is fine. Sure, you may run into
some performance problems eventually, and as you get more experience, you'll start
writing cleaner code, but for the Coding Challenges and the prototypes that you cre-
ate after reading this book, it is far more important that the game runs and is fun than
that the code is pretty. You can always go back and refactor it later to make it look and
perform better, but the most important thing is getting the game working at all. Then you
can playtest it and work on making it a better experience to play before you devote time
to improving the code.

Way back in Unity 4, there was a great sample project called Angry Bots that would

SWITCHING TO THE LIGHT EDITOR THEME (OPTIONAL)
Unlike Figure 17.3, all the other figures in this book use the Light Editor Theme.
It looks a lot better in print than the dark theme shown in Figure 17.3. You are,
of course, welcome to use whichever you want. If you do want to use the Light
theme like I do:
1. The first step is different depending on your operating system:
a. macOS: From the main menu bar, choose Unity > Preferences…
b. Windows: From the main menu bar, choose Edit > Preferences…
2. Click the General heading on the left side of the Preferences window.

to the Light theme.
Learning Your Way Around Unity
Before you can really get into coding things, you need to get to know the various win-
dow panes that you've just arranged. Refer to Figure 17.4 as you read about each pane.
Of course, your windows aren't yet in this arrangement, but they will be soon.

menu and labels for each window pane (showing Unity's Adventure demo project)

■ Scene/Prefab pane: The Scene pane allows you to navigate around your scene
in 3D and to select, move, rotate, and scale objects. I have added the Prefab desig-
nation here because this pane also has a second mode that is used to edit prefabs
(which are reusable molds from which any number of instances/copies can be made;
for example, you could create an Enemy prefab from which any number of Enemies
could be instantiated in the scene).
■ Game pane: The Game pane is where you preview your actual gameplay. This pane
also shows you the view from the Main Camera in your scene.
■ Hierarchy pane: The Hierarchy pane shows you every GameObject that is included
in your current scene. For now, you can think of each scene as a level of your game.
Everything that exists in your scene, from the camera to your player-character, is a

LANGUAGE: C#
This chapter introduces you to the key features
of C# and describes some important reasons
why it was chosen as the language for Unity.
It also examines the basic syntax of C#,
explaining what is meant by the structure of
some simple C# statements.
By the end of this chapter, you will better
understand C# and be ready to tackle the more
in-depth chapters that follow.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
348 CHAPTER 18 IntrodUCInG oUr lanGUaGe: C#
Understanding the Features of C#
As covered in Chapter 16, "Thinking in Digital Systems," programming consists of giving
the computer a series of simple commands, and C# (pronounced "see sharp") is the lan-
guage through which we will do so. However, many different programming languages
exist, each of which has benefits and drawbacks. Some of the features of C# are that it is
■ A compiled language
■ Managed code
■ Statically typed
■ Function based
■ Object oriented
Each of these features is described further in the following sections, and each will help
you in various ways.
C# Is a Compiled Language
When most people write computer programs, they are not actually writing in a
language that the computer itself understands. In fact, each computer chip on the
market has a slightly different set of very simple commands that it understands, known
as machine language. This language is very, very fast for the chip to execute, but it is
incredibly difficult for a person to read. For example, the machine language line
 1 1 11  1 would certainly mean something to the
right computer chip, but it means next to nothing to human readers. You might have
noticed, however, that every character of that machine code is either a 0 or 1. That's
because all the more complex types of data—numbers, letters, and so on—have been
converted down to individual bits of data (i.e., ones or zeros). If you've ever heard of
people programming computers using punch cards, this is exactly what they were
doing: For most formats of binary punch cards, physically punching a hole in card stock
represented a one, and an unpunched hole represented a zero.
For people to be able to write code more easily, human-readable programming
languages—sometimes called authoring languages —were created. You can think of an
authoring language as an intermediate language meant to act as a go-between from
you to the computer. Authoring languages such as C# are logical and simple enough for
a computer to interpret while also being close enough to written human languages to
allow programmers to easily read and understand them.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
UnderstandInG the FeatUres oF C# 349
Figure 18.1 A simple taxonomy of programming languages

57916.sourceSearchName: introductiontogamedesignprototypinganddevelopment3e introductionto game design prototyping and development from concept to playable game with unity and c
57916.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57916.heading: LANGUAGE: C#
57916.content:
A major division also exists in authoring languages between compiled languages such
as BASIC, C++, C#, and Java and interpreted languages such as JavaScript, Perl, PHP, and
Python (see Figure 18.1).
In an interpreted language, authoring and executing code is a two-step process:
■ The programmer writes the code.
■ Each time a player plays the game, the code is converted from the authoring lan-
guage to machine language in real time on the player's machine.
The good thing about this is that it enables code portability, because the authoring
code can be interpreted specifically for the type of computer on which it is running. For
example, the JavaScript of a given web page will run on almost any modern computer
regardless of whether the computer is running macOS, Windows, Linux, or one of many
mobile operating systems like iOS, Android, and so on. However, this flexibility also
causes the code to execute more slowly due to the time required to interpret the code
on the player's computer, the authoring language not being well optimized for the
device on which it will run, and a host of other reasons. Because the same interpreted
code is run on all devices, optimizing for the specific device on which it happens to be
running is impossible. This is the reason why 3D games created in an interpreted lan-
guage like JavaScript generally run much more slowly than those created in a compiled
language, even when running on the same computer.
In a compiled language, such as C#, the programming process comprises three separate
steps:
■ The programmer writes the code in an authoring language like C#.
■ A compiler converts the code from an authoring language to a compiled application
in machine language for a specific kind of machine.
■ Each time a player plays the game, their computer executes the compiled application.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
350 CHAPTER 18 IntrodUCInG oUr lanGUaGe: C#
This added middle process of compilation converts the code from the authoring lan-
guage into an executable (i.e., an application or app) that a computer can run directly
without needing an interpreter. Because the compiler has both a complete understand-
ing of the program and a complete understanding of the execution platform on which
the program will run, it is able to incorporate many optimizations into the process. In
games, these optimizations translate directly into higher frame rates, more detailed
graphics, and more responsive interactions. Most high-budget games are authored in a
compiled language because of this optimization and speed advantage, but this means
that a different executable must be compiled for each execution platform.
In many cases, compiled authoring languages are only suited for specific execution plat-

57917.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57917.heading: LANGUAGE: C#
57917.content:
forms. For instance, Objective-C is Apple Computer's proprietary authoring language for
making applications for both macOS and iOS. This language is based on C (a predeces-
sor of C++), but it includes a number of features that are unique to macOS or iOS devel-
opment. Similarly, XNA was a flavor of C# developed by Microsoft several years ago to
enable students to author games for both Windows-based personal computers and the
Xbox 360.
In the early versions of Unity, programmers were able to use any of three different
authoring languages: C#, a JavaScript flavor named UnityScript, or another interpreted
language named Boo. Unity gradually dropped Boo and then JavaScript because focus-
ing on C# allowed Unity to make great improvements in the speed at which the com-
piled code ran.
When compiling C# code, there are several different steps for Unity to perform, depend-
ing on the platform for which the code is being compiled. Initially, C# code is compiled
into an Intermediate Language. This Intermediate Language improves the portability of
Unity code and is able to be run through different scripting backends and compilation
processes to target any number of platforms, from iOS to Android, macOS, Windows
PC, interpreted languages such as WebGL (a specific form of JavaScript used in web
pages), and even game consoles such as the PlayStation, Switch, and Xbox.
The ability to write once and compile anywhere is not unique to Unity, but it is one of Unity
Technologies' core goals for the Unity game engine, and it is better integrated into Unity
than any other game development software I have seen. However, as a game designer,
you will still need to think seriously about the design differences between a game meant
for a handheld phone controlled by touch, a game meant to run on a personal computer
controlled by mouse and keyboard, or a game built for virtual or augmented reality, so you
will usually have slightly different code for the different platforms.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
UnderstandInG the FeatUres oF C# 351
C# Is Managed Code
More traditional compiled languages such as BASIC, C++, and Objective-C require
programmers to directly manage computer memory, obliging a programmer to manually
allocate and deallocate memory any time they create or destroy a variable.
1
If a programmer
doesn't manually deallocate RAM in these languages, their program will have a "memory
leak" and eventually allocate too much of the computer's RAM, causing it to crash.
Luckily for us, C# is managed code, which means that the allocation and de-allocation of
memory is handled automatically.
2
You can still cause memory leaks in managed code,
but it is more difficult to do so accidentally.
C# Is Statically Typed
Later chapters cover variables in more detail, but you should know a couple of things

57918.sourceSearchName: introductiontogamedesignprototypinganddevelopment3e introductionto game design prototyping and development from concept to playable game with unity and c
57918.title: Introductionto Game; Design , Prototyping , and Development; From Concept to Playable Game with Unity and C#
57918.heading: LANGUAGE: C#
57918.content:
about them now. First, a variable is just a named container for a value. For instance, in
algebra, you might have seen an expression like this:
[ 
In this one line, you have created a variable, named it [, and assigned it the value .
Later, if I asked you the value of [  , I'm sure you could tell me that the answer is 
because you remember that [ was holding the value  and know to add  to that value.
That is exactly what variables do for you in programming.
In most interpreted languages, like JavaScript, a single variable can hold any kind of
data. The variable [ could hold the number  one minute, an image the next, and a
sound file thereafter. This capability to hold any kind of value is what is meant when
we say that a programming language is dynamically typed, because the type of a vari-
able is determined based on what happens to be in it at run time, rather than being
predefined.
1. Memory allocation is the process of setting aside a certain amount of random-access memory
(RAM) in the computer to enable it to hold a chunk of data. Although computers now often
have hundreds of gigabytes (GB) of hard drive space, they still usually have less than 40GB of
RAM. RAM is much faster than hard drive memory, so all applications pull assets like images
and sounds from the hard drive, allocate some space for them in RAM, and then store them
in RAM for fast access.
2. One disadvantage of managed code is that it makes controlling exactly when memory is deal-
located and reclaimed very difficult. Instead, memory is automatically reclaimed in a process
called garbage collection. This can sometimes lead to a hitch in the frame rate of a game
on less powerful devices such as cell phones, but it's usually not noticeable, and Unity has
recently made improvements in incremental garbage collection to reduce this issue. Addition-
ally, unlike regular C# code, you will need to manually allocate and deallocate memory if
you choose to use Unity's Data-Oriented Technology Stack to write highly performant multi-
threaded code (as shown in Chapter 28, "Data-Oriented Design").
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

C#, in contrast, is statically typed. This means that when you initially create a variable,
you must tell it at that moment what kind of value it can hold:
int [ ;
In the preceding statement, you have created a variable named [ that it is exclusively
allowed to hold integer values (i.e., positive or negative numbers without a decimal
point), and assigned it the integer value . Although it might seem like static typing
would make programming more difficult, the use of static types enables the compiler
to make several optimizations and makes it possible for the authoring environment,

57919.heading: LANGUAGE: C#
57919.content:
Visual Studio, to perform real-time syntax checking on the code you write (much like
the grammar checking that is performed by Microsoft Word). This also enables and
enhances code-completion, a technology that enables Visual Studio to predict the
words you're typing and provide you with valid completion options based on the other
code that you've written. With code-completion, if you're typing and see the author-
ing environment suggest the correct completion of the word, you simply press Tab to
accept the suggestion. When you've become used to this, it can save you hundreds of
keystrokes every minute.
C# Is Function-Based
In the early days of programming, a program was composed of a single series of com-
mands. These programs were run directly from beginning to end much like the direc-
tions you would give to a friend who was trying to drive to your house:
1. From school, head north on Vermont.
2. Head west on I-10 for about 7.5 miles.
3. At the intersection with I-405, take the 405 south for 2 miles.
4. Take the exit for Venice Blvd.
5. Turn right onto Sawtelle Blvd.
6. My place is just north of Venice on Sawtelle.
As authoring languages improved, repeatable sections were added to programming in
the form of things like loops (a section of code that repeats itself) and subroutines (an oth-
erwise inaccessible section of code that is jumped to, executed, and then returned from).
The development of function-based procedural languages
3
allowed programmers to
name chunks of code and thereby encapsulate functionality (i.e., group a series of
actions under a single function name). For example, if in addition to giving someone
3. There are also functional languages such as Lisp, Scheme, Mathematica (Wolfram Language),
and Haskell, but for these functional languages, "functional" means something different than
the capabilities we have in C#.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
UnderstandInG the FeatUres oF C# 353
detailed directions to your house as described in the preceding list, you also asked them
to pick up some milk for you on the way, they would know that if they saw a grocery
store on the way, they should stop the car, get out, walk to find milk, pay for it, return to
their car, and continue on their way to your house. Because your friend already knows
how to buy milk, you just need to request that they do so rather than giving them
explicit instructions for every tiny step. This could look something like this:
"Could you please BuySoPeMilN() on your way over?"
This statement encapsulates all the instructions to buy milk into the single function
named BuySoPeMilN(). You can do the same thing in any procedural language. When
the computer is processing C# and encounters a function name followed by paren-

57920.heading: LANGUAGE: C#
57920.content:
theses, it will call that function (i.e., it will execute all the actions encapsulated in the
function). You will learn much more about functions in Chapter 24, "Functions and
Parameters."
The other fantastic thing about functions is that after you have written the code for
the function BuySoPeMilN() one time, you should never have to write it again. Even
if you're working on a completely different program, you can often copy and paste
functions like BuySoPeMilN() and reuse them without having to write the whole thing
again from scratch. The C# script named 8tils.cs that you will see in several of the
tutorials in this book includes several reusable functions.
C# Is Object-Oriented
Many years after functions were invented, the idea of Object-Oriented Programming
(OOP) was created. In OOP, not only functionality but also data are encapsulated
together into something called an object, or more correctly a class. This is covered
extensively in Chapter 26, "Classes," but here's a metaphor for now.
Consider a group of various animals. Each animal has specific data that it knows about
itself. Some elements of this data could be its species, age, size, emotional state, level of
hunger, current location, and so on. Each animal also has certain things that it can do:
eat, move, breath, etc. The data elements for each animal are analogous to variables in
code, and the actions that the animal can perform are analogous to functions.
Before OOP, an animal represented in code could hold data (i.e., variables) but could not
perform any actions. Those actions were performed by functions that were not directly
connected to the animal. A programmer could write a function named MoYe() that
could move any kind of animal, but they would have to write several lines of code in that
function that determined what kind of animal it was and what type of movement was
appropriate for it. For example, dogs walk, fish swim, and birds fly. Any time the pro-
grammer added a new animal, they were required to change MoYe() to accommodate
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

57921.content:
354 CHAPTER 18 INTRODUCING OUR LANGUAGE: C#
the new type of locomotion, and MoYe() would thereby grow larger and more complex
with the addition of each new animal.
Object orientation changed all of this by introducing the ideas of classes and class
inheritance. A class combines both variables and functions into one whole object. In OOP,
instead of having a huge MoYe() function that can handle any animal, a much smaller and
more specific MoYe() function is attached to each animal. This eliminates the need for a
programmer to expand MoYe() every time they add a new type of animal, and it eliminates
the need for all the type-checking of animal types in the non-OOP version of MoYe().
Instead, each new animal class is given its own small MoYe() function when it is created.
Object orientation also includes the concept of class inheritance. This enables classes
to have subclasses that are more specific, and it allows the subclasses to either inherit
or override functions in their superclasses. Through inheritance, a single $niPal class
could be created that included declarations of all the types of data that are shared by
all animals: age, size, and the others listed earlier. This class would also have a MoYe()
function, but it would be nonspecific. In subclasses of $niPal, like Dog or )ish,
the function MoYe() could be overridden to cause specific behavior like walking or
swimming. This is a key element of modern game programming, and it will serve you
well when you want to create something like a basic EnePy class that is then further
specified into various subclasses for each individual enemy type that you want to create.

While there are many benefits to Object-Oriented Programming, one place that it fails is
in regard to efficient memory usage and organization. Another is that it is very difficult
to write multithreaded object-oriented code. An alternative to OOP that has been gain-
ing traction lately is Data-Oriented Design (DOD). Data-Oriented Design is a different
approach to designing code that is based around efficient memory management and
ease of multithreading. Starting in 2018, Unity began creating its Data-Oriented Tech
Stack (DOTS), which comprises three core elements:
■ Entity Component System: A method of designing code that takes full advantage
of Data-Oriented Design.
■ The Job System: A library of code that makes multithreading in Unity C# much
easier.
■ The Burst Compiler: By limiting some of the less-efficient aspects of C#, Unity was
able to create a compiler that could make much faster and more efficient machine
language code from C#.
Taken together, DOTS can make Unity code not only much faster but also more effi-
cient, both in terms of the temperature of the processor and battery life. DOTS is still

Reading and Understanding C# Syntax
Just like any other language, C# has a specific syntax that you must follow. Take a look at
these example statements in English:
■ ■ The dog barked at the squirrel.
■ ■ At the squirrel the dog barked.
■ ■ The dog at the squirrel. barked
■ ■ barked The dog at the squirrel.
Each of these English statements has the same words and punctuation, but they are
in a different order, and the punctuation and capitalization are changed. Because you
are familiar with the English language, you can easily tell that only the first is worded
correctly. Another way of examining this is to look at it more abstractly as just the parts
of speech:
■ ■ [Subject] [verb] [object].
■ ■ [Object] [subject] [verb].
■ ■ [Subject] [object]. [verb]
■ ■ [verb] [Subject] [object].
When parts of speech are rearranged like this, doing so alters the syntax of the sentence,
and the latter three sentences are incorrect because they have syntax errors.
Just like any language, C# has specific syntax rules for how statements must be written.
Let's examine this simple statement in detail:
int x = 5;
As explained earlier, this statement does several things:
■ ■ Declares a variable named x of the type int
Any time a statement starts with a variable type, the second word of the statement
becomes the name of a new variable of that type (see Chapter 20, "Variables and
Components"). This is called declaring a variable.

The symbol is used to assign values to variables (which is also called initializing a
variable if it is the first time that any value has been assigned to the variable). When
you do this, the variable name is on the left, and the value assigned is on the right.
■ Ends with a semicolon (;)
Every simple statement in C# must end with a semicolon (;). This is similar in use to
the period at the end of sentences in the English language.

Why not end C# statements with a period? Computer programming lan-

ments in C# because it is already in use in numbers as a decimal point (for
example, the period in .11). For clarity, the only use of the semicolon
in C# is to end statements.

4. Click Cube in the Hierarchy pane, and you should see it selected with an orange

Figure 19.8). The primary purpose of the Inspector pane is to enable you to view
and edit the components that make up any GameObject. This Cube GameObject has
Transform, Mesh Filter, Box Collider, and Mesh Renderer components:
■ Transform: The Transform component sets the position, rotation, and scale
of the GameObject. This is the only component that is required in every
GameObject.
■ Cube (Mesh Filter): The Mesh Filter component gives the GameObject its
three-dimensional shape, which is modeled as a mesh composed of triangles. 3D
models in games are generally a surface that is hollow inside. Unlike a real egg
(which is filled with a yolk and albumen), a 3D model of an egg would just be a
mesh simulating an empty eggshell. The Mesh Filter component attaches a 3D
model to the GameObject. In the case of Cube, the Mesh Filter is using a simple
3D cube model that is built into Unity, but you can also import complex 3D
models into the Project pane to bring more complex meshes into your game.
■ Box Collider: Collider components enable a GameObject to interact with other
objects in the physics simulation that Unity runs. The PhysX physics engine in
Unity uses several different kinds of colliders, including Sphere, Capsule, Box,
and Mesh (in increasing order of computational complexity; i.e., a Mesh
Collider is much more difficult for the computer to calculate than a Box Collider).

CHANGING THE SCENE VIEW
The first tool on the toolbar shown in Figure 19.13—known as the Hand Tool —is
used to manipulate the view shown in the Scene pane. The Scene pane has its
own invisible scene camera that is different from the Main Camera in the Hierar-
chy. The Hand Tool has several different abilities. Select the Hand Tool (by either
clicking it or pressing Q on your keyboard) and try the following:
■ Left-dragging (i.e., clicking and dragging using the left mouse button) in
the Scene pane moves the position of the scene camera left, right, up, or
down without changing the position of any of the objects in the scene.
To be technical, the scene camera is moved in a plane perpendicular to
the direction that the camera is facing (i.e., perpendicular to the camera's
forward vector).
■ Right-dragging in the Scene pane rotates the scene camera to look in
the direction of your drag. The scene camera stays in the same position
when right-dragging.
■ Holding the Option key on macOS (Alt key on a PC) changes the cur-
sor over the Scene pane from a hand to an eye, and left-dragging with
the Option key held causes the Scene view to rotate around objects in
the Scene pane. This is known as orbiting the camera around the scene.
When orbiting, the position of the scene camera changes, but the loca-
tion that the scene camera is looking at does not.
■ Scrolling with the scroll wheel on your mouse causes the scene camera
to zoom in and out of the scene. You can also zoom by Option+right-
dragging in the Scene pane.
The best way to get a feel for the Hand Tool is to try moving around the scene
using the different methods described in this sidebar. After you have played with
it a little, it should become second nature to you.

Statically Typed Variables in C#
Instead of being able to be assign any kind of value to any variable, C# variables are
statically typed, meaning that they can only accept a specific type of value, and that type
must be declared before the variable can be used.

This is necessary because the com-
puter needs to know how much space in memory to allocate to each variable. A large
image can take up many megabytes or even gigabytes of space, whereas a Boolean
value (which can only hold either a 1 or a 0) only really requires a single bit. Even just
a single megabyte is equivalent to 8,388,608 bits! One of the major benefits of static
typing is that it allows the compiler to discover many kinds of errors at compile time

Declaring a variable creates it, gives it a name and type, and allocates space in memory

these declared variables:

Bools are extremely useful for logic operations such as if statements and
other conditionals, which are covered in the next two chapters. In C#, bool literals are

in Unity can store a number between –2,147,483,648 and 2,147,483,647 with 1 bit used
for the positive or negative sign of the number and 31 bits used for the numerical value.
An int can hold any integer value between these two numbers (inclusive):

The Scope of Variables
In addition to variable type, another important concept for variables is scope. The scope
of a variable refers to the range of code in which the variable exists and is understood.
If you declare a variable in one part of your code, it might not have meaning in another
part. This is a complex issue that will be covered throughout this book. If you want to
learn about it progressively, just read the book in order. If you want to get a lot more
information about variable scope right now, you can read the section "Variable Scope"
in Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."
Naming Conventions
The code in this book follows a number of rules governing the naming of variables,
functions, classes, and so on. Although none of these rules are mandatory, following
them will make your code more readable not only to others who try to decipher it but
also to yourself if you ever need to return to it months later and hope to understand
what you wrote. Every coder follows slightly different rules—my personal rules have
even changed over the years—but the rules I present here have worked well for both me
and my students, and they are consistent with most C# code that I've encountered in
Unity:
1. Use camelCase for pretty much everything (see the "CamelCase" sidebar).

CAMELCASE
CamelCase is a common way of writing variable names in programming. It allows
the programmer or someone reading their code to easily parse long variable
names. Here are some examples:
■ aVeryLongNameThatIsEasierToReadBecauseOfCamelCase
■ variableNamesStartWithALowerCaseLetter
■ ClassNamesStartWithACapitalLetter
The key feature of camelCase is that it allows multiple words to be combined into
one with a medial capital letter at the beginning of each original word. It is named
camelCase because it looks a bit like the humps on a camel's back.
2. Variable names should start with a lowercase letter (e.g., soPe9ariable1aPe).

can see, snake_case combines multiple words with an underscore in between them.
For your later reference, this information is repeated and expanded in the "Naming

variable that defines red for the entire class Color; as a result, red has the same

Quaternion: Rotation Information
Explaining the inner workings of the Quaternion
13
class is far beyond the scope of this
book, but you will be using them often to set and adjust the rotation of objects through
the Quaternion GaPe2bMect.transforP.rotation, which is part of every GameObject.
Quaternions define rotations in a way that avoids gimbal lock. Gimbal lock occurs when
one rotation axis aligns with another, thereby limiting rotation possibilities and is a prob-
lem with standard x, y, z (or Euler, pronounced "oiler") rotations. Most of the time, you
will be defining a Quaternion by passing in Euler rotations and allowing Unity to convert
them into the equivalent Quaternion:
Quaternion lookUp45Deg = 4uaternion.Euler( f f f );
In cases like this, the three floats passed into 4uaternion.Euler() are the number of
degrees to rotate around the x, y, and z axes (respectively colored red, green, and blue
in Unity). GameObjects, including the Main Camera in a scene, are initially oriented to
be looking down the positive z-axis. The rotation in the preceding code would rotate
the camera –45 degrees around the red x-axis, causing it to then be looking up at a
45 ° angle relative to the positive z-axis. If that last sentence was confusing, don't worry
about it too much right now. Later, you can try going into Unity and changing the x, y,
and z rotation values in the Transform Inspector for a GameObject and see how it alters
the object's orientation.

Transform

handles critical GameObject information like position (the location of the GameObject),

AND CONDITIONALS
Most people have heard that computer data
is, at its base level, composed entirely of 1s
and 0s—bits that are either true or false.
However, only programmers really understand
how much of programming is about boiling a
problem down to a true or false value and then
responding to it.
In this chapter, you learn about Boolean
operations like AND, OR, and NOT; you learn
about comparison statements like >, <, ==, and
!=; and you come to understand conditionals
like if and sZitch. These all lay at the heart of
programming.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
406 CHAPTER 21 Boolean oPeratIons and CondItIonals
Booleans
As you learned in the previous chapter, a bool is a variable that can hold a value of either
true or false. Booleans were named after George Boole, a mathematician who worked
with true and false values and logical operations (now known as "Boolean operations").
Though computers did not exist at the time of his research, computer logic was funda-
mentally based on it, because each transistor in a computer processor can have a state
of either on or off (i.e., true or false).
In C# programming, bools are used to store simple information about the state of the
game (for example, bool gaPe2Yer false ) and to control the flow of the program
through the if and sZitch statements covered later in this chapter.
Boolean Operations
Boolean operations allow programmers to modify or combine bool variables in mean-
ingful ways.
 (The NOT Operator)
The  (either pronounced "not" or "bang") operator reverses the value of a bool. False
becomes true, and true becomes false:
print(  true ); // Output: false
print(  false ); // Output: true
print(  ( true) ); // Output: true (the double negative of true is true)
 is also sometimes referred to as the logical negation operator to differentiate it from
a (the bitwise not operator), which is explained in the "Bitwise Boolean Operators and
Layer Masks" section of Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."
(The AND Operator)
The operator returns true only if both operands are true:
print( false false ); // false
print( false true ); // false
print( true false ); // false
print( true true ); // true
__ (The OR Operator)
The __ operator returns true if either operand is true as well as if both are true:
print( false __ false ); // false
print( false __ true ); // true
print( true __ false ); // true
print( true __ true ); // true

Combination of Boolean Operations
It is often useful to combine various Boolean operations in a single line:

ALWAYS USE PARENTHESES IN YOUR CODE! Regardless of the order

as possible. Good readability is essential in your code if you ever plan to
work with someone else (or even if you want to read the same code yourself
weeks or months later). I code by a simple rule: If there's any chance at all
that something might be misunderstood later, I use parentheses and add
comments to clarify what I am doing in the code and how it will be inter-
preted by the computer.
Logical Equivalence of Boolean Operations
The surprising depth of Boolean logic is beyond the scope of this book, but with even a
little knowledge of Boolean logic, you can accomplish some very interesting things by
combining Boolean operations. In the examples of logic rules that follow, a and b are

regardless of whether the shorting or non-shorting operators are used:

APPROXIMATE FLOAT COMPARISON
Because float numbers are sometimes inaccurate, there is a Mathf method for
determining whether the two numbers are approximately equal.
print( 0.1f == ( 1.0f/10.0f ) ); // Sometimes true, sometimes false!
print( Mathf.Approximately( 0.1f, (1.0f / 10.0f) ) ); // Always true
Unity states that the statement with the == operator will return true or false
based on the circumstances, which is not ideal. So, they provide the static Mathf.
$ppro[iPately() method, which will always return true in that situation. How-
ever, you have no control over how approximate Mathf.$ppro[iPately() is, so
I prefer another solution.
print( Mathf.Approximately( 3.14f, Mathf.PI ) ); // Still false
print( CloseEnough( 3.14f, Mathf.PI, 0.01f ) ); // true!
bool CloseEnough( float a, float b, float diff ) {
return ( Mathf.Abs( a - b ) < diff );
}
Here, I've written a &loseEnough() method that subtracts b from a and then
checks to see whether the absolute value of the difference is less than the diff that
was passed in. This method gives you control over how close the values need to be.
See the "Testing Equality by Value or Reference" sidebar for more detailed information
about how equality is handled for several different variable types.

Unity's version of C# will compare most simple data types by value. This means
that as long as the values of the two variables are the same, they will be seen as
equivalent. This works for all the following data types:
Q bool Q string

However, with more complex variable types such as GaPe2bMect, Material,
Renderer, and so on, C# instead checks equality by reference. When comparing
equality by reference, it does not compare whether the values of the two variables
are equal but instead checks to see whether the references of the two variables are
equal. In other words, it checks to see whether the two variables are referencing
(or pointing to) the same single object in the computer's memory. In the follow-
ing example of comparison by reference, we'll assume that bo[Prefab is a pre-
existing variable that references a GameObject prefab.
2

and so on), the operator sees them as different because they are actually two
different objects, and therefore reside in two different places in memory. go and
go are seen as equal by because they both refer to the same object in memory.
Let's continue the previous code:
go0.transform.position = new Vector3( 10, 20, 30 );

instance, its position remains the same. However, because go and go reference
the same GameObject instance, go.transforP.position reflects the change as
well.

Conditional Statements
Conditional statements can be combined with bool values and comparison operators
to control the flow of your programs. This means that a true value can cause the code to
generate one result whereas a false value can cause it to generate another. It also means
that a true value could cause one branch of code to execute, but a false would cause
another branch to execute. The two most common forms of conditional statements are
if and sZitch.
if Statements
An if statement will only execute the code inside its braces ^} if the value inside its
parentheses () evaluates to true:
if (true) {
print( "The code in the first if statement was executed." );
}
if (false) {
print( "The code in the second if statement was executed." );
}
// The output of this code will be:
// The code in the first if statement was executed.
The code inside the braces ^} of the first if statement executes, yet the code inside the
braces of the second if statement does not.
note
Statements enclosed in braces do not require a semicolon after the closing
brace. Other statements that have been covered in this book all require a
semicolon at the end:
float approxPi = 3.14159f; // This statement needs a semicolon
Compound statements (that is, those surrounded by braces) do not require
a semicolon after the closing brace:
if (true) {
print( "Hello" ); // This line needs a semicolon.
print( "World" ); // This line needs a semicolon.
} // No semicolon required after the closing brace!
The same is true for any compound statement surrounded by braces.

57983.content:
LOOPS
Computer programs are usually designed to do
the same thing repeatedly. In a standard game
loop, the game draws a frame to the screen,
takes input from the player, considers that
input, and then draws the next frame, repeating
this behavior at least 30 times every second.
A loop in C# code causes the computer to
repeat a certain behavior several times. This
could be anything from looping over every
enemy in the scene and considering the AI of
each to looping over all the physics objects in
a scene and checking for collisions. By the end
of this chapter, you'll understand all you need
to know about loops, and in the next chapter,
you'll learn how to use them with arrays.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
424 CHAPTER 22 looPs
Types of Loops
C# has only four kinds of loops: Zhile, doڕZhile, for, and foreach. Of those, you'll be
using for and foreach much more often than the others because they are generally
safer and more adaptable to the challenges you'll encounter when making games:
Q Zhile loop: The most basic type of loop. Checks a condition before each loop to
determine whether to continue looping.
Q doڕZhile loop: Similar to the Zhile loop but checks a condition after each loop to
determine whether to continue looping.
Q for loop: A loop statement that includes an initializing statement, a variable that
increments with each iteration, and an end condition. The most commonly used
loop structure.
Q foreach loop: A loop statement that automatically iterates over every element of an
enumerable object or collection. This chapter contains some discussion of foreach,
and it is covered more extensively in the next chapter as part of the discussion of the
various C# collections.
Unity also has several different game loops, which are methods in your code that are
called on a regular or repeating basis. These include 8pdate(), )i[ed8pdate(), and
/ate8pdate() among others, but they are part of how Unity works—not part of C#—so
they will be covered much more in Part III of the book.

HOW TO FORCE QUIT AN APPLICATION
Implement a force quit by doing the following:
On macOS
1. Press Command-Option-Esc on the keyboard. The Force Quit window appears.
2. Find the application that is misbehaving. Its name will often be followed by
"(not responding)" in the applications list.
3. Click that application name in the list, and then click Force Quit. You may
need to wait a few seconds for the force quit to happen.
On Windows
1. Press Shift+Control+Esc on the keyboard. The Windows Task Manager opens.

3. Click that application, and then click End Task. You may need to wait a few

INCREMENT AND DECREMENT OPERATORS
Line 10 of Code Listing 22.2 includes the first instance in this book of the incre-
ment operator (). The increment operator increases the value of the variable that
it follows by 1. So, if i , then the i; statement would set the value of i to .
There is also a decrement operator (). The decrement operator decreases the
value of the variable by 1.
You can place increment and decrement operators either before or after the
variable name, and doing so causes the statement to be treated differently (i.e.,
i and i act slightly differently). The difference is in whether the initial value
is returned (i) or whether the incremented value is returned (i). Here's an
example to clarify.
7 void Start() {
8 int i = 1;
9 print( i ); // Output: 1
10 print( i++ ); // Output: 1
11 print( i ); // Output: 2
12 print( ++i ); // Output: 3
13 }
As you can see, line 9 prints the current value of i, which is 1. Then, on line 10,
you can think of the post-increment operator i as first returning the current
value of i, which is printed (resulting in the 1), and then incrementing the i, set-
ting its value to 2.
Line 11 prints the current value of i, which is 2. Then, on line 12, the pre-increment
operator i first increments the value of i from 2 to 3 and then returns it to the
print function, which prints a 3.
tip
In most of the examples in this chapter, the iteration variable used will be
named i. The variable names i, M, and N are often used by programmers
as iteration variables (i.e., the variable that increments in a loop), and as
a result, they are rarely used in any other code situations. Because these
variables are created and destroyed so often in various loop structures, you
should avoid using the variable names i, M, or N for anything else.

for Loops
In both the Zhile and doڕZhile examples, we needed to declare and define a variable
i, increment the variable i, and then check the condition clause on the variable i; and
each of these actions was performed by a separate statement. The for loop handles all
of these actions in a single line.

The for loop in this example sends the same output to the Console pane as was sent by
the "more useful" Zhile loop (in Code Listing 22.2), yet it does so in fewer lines of code.
The structure of a for loop requires an initialization clause, a condition clause, and an
iteration clause to be valid. In the above example, the three clauses are as follows:
Initialization clause: for ( int i ; i<3; i++ ) {
Condition clause: for ( int i=0; i; i++ ) {
Iteration clause: for ( int i=0; i<3; i ) {
The initialization clause ( int i ; ) is executed before the for loop begins.
It declares and defines a variable that is scoped locally to the for loop. This means
that the int i in the initialization clause will cease to exist when the for loop is
complete. For more information on variable scoping, see the "Variable Scope" section
of Appendix B, "Useful Concepts."
The condition clause ( i ) is checked before every iteration of the for loop, includ-
ing the first iteration (just as the condition clause is checked before the first iteration of a
Zhile loop). If the condition clause is true, the code between the braces of the for loop
is executed.
The iteration clause ( i ) is executed after each iteration of the code between the
braces of the for loop has completed (i.e., after each time that the lines between the
braces { } of the for loop execute—in this case, the single line print( /oop   i ); —
the i is executed).
After the iteration clause executes, the condition clause is checked again, and if the
condition clause is still true, the code between the braces is executed again, and the
iteration clause is executed again. This continues until the condition clause evaluates to
false, at which point the for loop ends.
Because for loops mandate that each of these three clauses be included and that they
all be on the same line, it is easier to avoid writing infinite loops when working with for
loops.

MODULO OPERATOR
Line 9 of Code Listing 22.10 for the continue jump statement is the first instance
in this book of the modulo operator ( ). Modulo (or more commonly, "mod")
returns the remainder of dividing one number by another. For example, 1   
would return a value of 2 because the remainder of 12/5 is 2 (5 goes into 12 two
times (5 × 2 = 10), leaving a remainder of 2).
Mod can also be used with floats, so 1.f   1f would return .f, because 1
goes into 12 twelve times, leaving 0.6 as the remainder.
Similarly, 1.f   .f would return .1f, because 0.5 goes into 12.6 twenty-
five times (0.5 × 25 = 12.5), leaving a remainder of 0.1.
However, because of the inaccuracy of float math, 1.f   .f could possibly
return .1f, which is not equal to .1f. If you are dealing with floats
and modulo, I highly recommend using approximate methods of comparing the
results. See the "Approximate Float Comparison" sidebar in Chapter 21, "Boolean
Operations and Conditionals," for more information.
Summary
Understanding loops is one of the key elements of becoming a good programmer.
However, it's fine if not all of this makes perfect sense now. After you start using loops
in the development of some actual game prototypes (like in Part III of this book!), it
will become more clear to you. Just make sure that you are actually typing each code
example into Unity and running it to help with your understanding of the material.
Also remember that in my coding, I commonly use for and foreach but rarely or never
use Zhile and doڕZhile because of the increased likelihood of Zhile and doڕZhile caus-
ing an infinite loop.
In the next chapter, you will learn about arrays and Lists, two forms of ordered
collections of similar items, and you will see how loops are used to iterate over these
collections. You will also learn about Dictionaries, a non-ordered collection, and some
other collections.

COLLECTIONS IN C#
C# collections enable you to act on several
similar things as a group. For example, you
could store all of the enemy GameObjects in
a List and loop over that List each frame to
update all of their positions and states.
This chapter covers three important types of
these collections in detail: Lists, arrays, and
Dictionaries. By the end of this chapter, you will
understand how these collection types work
and which to use in various situations.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
438 CHAPTER 23 ColleCtIons In C#
C# Collections
A collection is a group of objects that are referenced by a single variable. In regular life,
collections would be things like a group of people, a pride of lions, a parliament of
rooks, or a murder of crows. Just like these animal grouping terms, the collections we'll
use in C# can only hold a single type of data
1
(e.g., you couldn't include a tiger in a
pride of lions). The array type is built in to C# at a low level, whereas the other collection
types here rely on the System.Collections.Generic code library to work, as described
later in the chapter. See the "What Is a Generic Collection?" sidebar for more informa-
tion on generics in C# and the meaning of T>.
WHAT IS A GENERIC COLLECTION?
Apart from the array, every other type of collection you see in this chapter is part
of the System.Collections.Generic code library. A generic collection in C# is one
that is designed to work with any type of data, as determined by the programmer.
With a generic, the type for the generic to work with is entered between angle
brackets >. For example:
■ /iststring> string/ist; — declares a List of strings
■ /istGaPe2bMect> go/ist; — declares a List of GameObjects
Throughout C# documentation and this chapter, you will see generic collections
described with T> as the type. In this case, the T is a stand-in for any type that
you would choose to put there in any code you write.
C# generics are also used in several other places, one of the most common Unity
examples of which is requesting a component that is attached to a GameObject.
The Get&oPponent() method is described in documentation as gaPe2bMect.
Get&oPponentT>(). Just as with the collections, the T> here is a stand-in for
whatever type of component you want to request. For example, gaPe2bMect.
Get&oPponentRigidbody>() requests the Rigidbody component that is
attached to gaPe2bMect.

Commonly Used Collections
The following is a brief overview of some of the most commonly used collections. The
array, List, and Dictionary types will be covered in much more depth later in this chapter
and used throughout the book. I include Queue and Stack so that you're aware of them,
but they are not used elsewhere in this book.
■ array: An array is an indexed, ordered list of objects. The length of an array must be

Following the standard project setup procedure, create a new project in Unity. If

Using Generic Collections
The beginning of all Unity C# scripts automatically includes three lines that start with
the word using.
using UnityEngine;
using System.Collections;
using System.Collections.Generic;
Each of these using lines loads a library of code and gives the script the ability to use
code within that library. The order of these lines doesn't matter, and the default order
has actually changed over the years. I've put them in this order to make it easier to
discuss them.
using 8nityEngine; is the most important library in Unity coding as it gives this C#
script knowledge of all the standard Unity objects, including things like MonoBehaviour,
GameObject, Rigidbody, Transform, and so on.

Choosing Whether to Use
an Array or List
Arrays and Lists are very similar, so people are often unsure which one to use in any
given situation. The primary differences between the array and List collection types are
as follows:
■ List has flexible length, whereas array length is more difficult to change.
■ Array allows multidimensional indices.
■ Array allows empty elements in the middle of the collection.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

gaPe2bMect.Get&oPponentsIn&hildrenTransforP>()), Unity will return an
array. Of course, if you need flexibility, you can easily convert this to a List.
Because they are simpler to implement and take less forethought (due to their flexible
length), I personally tend to use Lists much more often than arrays. This is especially
true when prototyping games, because prototyping requires a lot of flexibility.

how to do so.

SET UP THE PROJECT FOR THIS CHAPTER
Following the standard project setup procedure, create a new project in Unity. For
information on the standard project setup procedure, see Appendix A.
Q Project Template: 3D Core
■ Project Name: Function Examples
■ Scene Name: _Scene_Functions
No need to make any scripts prior to starting the project.
Definition of a Function
You've actually been writing functions since your first Hello World program, but up
until now, you've been adding content to built-in Unity MonoBehaviour functions like
Start() and 8pdate(). From now on, you'll also be writing functions with custom
names.
The best way to think about a function is as a chunk of code that does something. As an
example, follow these steps to create a script that will count the number of times that
8pdate() has been called:
1. Add a new Cube to the scene: From the Unity menu bar, choose GameObject > 3D
Object > Cube.
2. Create a new C# script named FunctionsEx and attach it to the Cube.
3. Open FunctionsEx in Visual Studio and add the bold lines of Code Listing 24.1:

In an actual game, Print8pdates() would not be a terribly useful function, but it does
showcase two of the important concepts covered in this chapter:
■ Functions encapsulate actions: You can think of a function as a named collection
of several lines of code. Every time the function is called, those lines of code are ex-
ecuted. This is demonstrated by both Print8pdates() and by the BuySoPeMilN()
example from Chapter 18, "Introducing Our Language: C#."
■ Functions contain their own scope: As you can read in the "Variable Scope"
section of Appendix B, "Useful Concepts," variables declared within a function have
their scope limited to that function. Therefore, the variable outputMessage (de-
clared on line 16) has a scope limited to just the function Print8pdates(). This can
either be stated as " outputMessage is scoped to the function Print8pdates() " or
" outputMessage is local to the function Print8pdates()."
Contrast the scope of the local variable outputMessage with that of the class field
nuPTiPes&alled, which has a scope of the entire )unctionsE[ class and can be
used by any function in )unctionsE[. (A variable that is scoped to an entire class is
called a field.)

Function Parameters and Arguments
Some functions are called with empty parentheses following them (e.g., Print8pdates()
in Code Listing 24.1). Other functions can be passed information in between the paren-
theses (e.g., Say(Hello) in Code Listing 24.3). When a function is designed to receive
outside information via the parentheses like this, the type of information is specified by
one or more parameters that create a local function variable (with a specific type) to hold
the information. In line 10 of Code Listing 24.3, Yoid Say( string sayThis ) declares a
parameter named sayThis that is of the string type. sayThis can then be used as a local
variable within the Say() function.
When information is sent to a function via its parameters, it is referred to as passing
information to the function. Each variable passed into a parameter is called an argument.
In line 7 of Code Listing 24.3, the function Say() is called with the argument Hello.
Another way to say this is that Hello is passed to the function Say(). The type of the
arguments passed to a function must match the parameter types of the function, or it
will cause an error.

58058.heading: DEBUGGING
58058.content:
DEBUGGING
To the uninitiated, debugging can seem like a
mystical art. On the contrary, it's actually one
of the best skills you can have as a developer,
though it's rarely taught to novice coders,
which I think is a tragic missed opportunity.
All coders make mistakes, and knowing about
debugging will enable you to find and correct
those mistakes much faster than just staring at
the code and hoping the bug will reveal itself.
By the end of this chapter, you'll understand
the difference between a compile-time error
and a runtime error, you'll know how to set
breakpoints in your code, and you'll know how
to step through the lines of your program one
at a time to help you root out hard-to-find
bugs.
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.
494 CHAPTER 25 deBUGGInG
Getting Started with Debugging
Before you can start finding bugs, you need to make some. For this chapter, you'll start
from the project you created for Chapter 19, "Hello World: Your First Program." If you
don't have that project on hand, you can always download it from this book's website:
http://book.prototools.net/
On the website, find Chapter 25, "Debugging," and click to download the project for
the beginning of the chapter.
Throughout this chapter, I instruct you to make a number of bugs on purpose. This
might seem like a strange way to do things, but my goal in doing so is to give you some
experience with tracking down and fixing several different kinds of bugs and other
errors you will almost certainly encounter while working with Unity. Each of these
example bugs will introduce you to a different kind of potential future problem and help
you understand how to go about finding and fixing bugs when you encounter them.
note
Throughout this chapter, I refer to errors occurring on specific line numbers.
Sometimes this will be the exact same line number that you get for the
error, and sometimes it might be shifted up or down by a couple lines. Don't
worry if you don't have exactly the same line numbers as I do; just look for
the content that I'm discussing near the line numbers that I reference.

58059.heading: 90% OF BUGS ARE JUST TYPOS
58059.content:
90% OF BUGS ARE JUST TYPOS
1
I've spent so much time helping
students fix bugs that now I can very quickly spot a typo in code. The most
common include the following:
■ Misspellings: If you type even one letter wrong, the computer
won't have any idea what you're talking about.
■ Capitalization: To your C# compiler, $ and a are two completely
different letters, so Yariable, 9ariable, and Yari$ble are all
completely different words.

■ Missing semicolons: Just like almost every sentence in English
should end in a period, nearly every statement in C# should end in
a semicolon (;). Leaving the semicolon out often causes an error
on the next line. C# and many other languages use a semicolon
because the period is already used for decimal numbers (e.g.,
.11) and what's called dot syntax in variable referencing (e.g.,
gaPe2bMect.transforP.position).
Compile-Time Bugs
A compile-time bug (or error) is a problem that Unity discovers when it is compiling C#
code (i.e., when it is attempting to interpret the C# code and turn it into the Common
Intermediate Language that is later converted by Unity to machine language that can
run on your computer).

intentionally cause a compile-time error and explore how they work:

automatically increment the name of the scene and call this new scene _Scene_2.
However, Unity recently changed how this works.

make a couple quick changes. (If you like how Unity numbers things now, you don't
need to do this and can just manually rename _Scene_1 1 to _Scene_2.)
a. From the menu bar, choose Edit > Project Settings…
b. Click the word Editor in the list on the left to access Unity Editor settings.
c. Scroll down all the way to the bottom where you'll find a Numbering Scheme
section.
d. Set Game Object Naming to Prefab_1.
e. Set Space Before Number in Asset Names to false (unchecked).
f. Close the Project Settings window.
g. Go ahead and delete _Scene_1 1.
h. Now, if you select _Scene_1 and attempt to duplicate it again, it should cor-
rectly increment to _Scene_2.

OPENING BRACE POSITIONING IN C# There are two standards for where
to place opening braces in C# (and most similar programming languages).

opening brace on the following line makes your code take up more space,
and if I did that throughout this book, it would be about 200 pages longer!

TINTING PLAY MODE IN UNITY Because of the frustration that can occur
when something that you changed in play mode gets reset as soon as you
exit play mode, many developers choose to tint their Unity window when-
ever it is playing. To do this:
1. From the main Unity menu, choose Unity > Preferences… (macOS)
Edit > Preferences… (Windows).
2. In the Preferences window, click Colors in the list on the left side.
3. Under the General heading in the Colors preferences, there is a
color for Playmode tint that is white by default.
The Playmode tint color is overlaid on the Unity editor window (but not the
Scene or Game panes) whenever you enter play mode. When the color is
white, it won't change anything, but setting it to another color will make it
much more obvious when Unity is playing.
Unity Errors (That Aren't Your Fault)
Because you are working with the 2020.3 LTS version of Unity, you will encounter these far
less frequently, but at some point in your time working with Unity, you will definitely see
errors pop up that are not your fault. These usually show up as red errors in the Console
pane, but they refer to aspects of Unity over which you have no control. This happened far
more frequently in the past, and I always recommend managing it in the same way:
1. If you see a red error appear in the Console pane that doesn't seem to be referring to
your code, click the Clear button near the top-left of the Console. If the error doesn't
come back (which is very frequently the case), then you're done!

58069.heading: HOW TO FORCE QUIT AN APPLICATION
58069.content:
HOW TO FORCE QUIT AN APPLICATION
Before getting too far into debugging, knowing how to force quit an application
(i.e., quit an application that won't respond to any user input) is useful. Some-
times, either Unity or Visual Studio will just stop responding, and you might need
to do this to quit the frozen application.
On a macOS Computer
Implement a force quit by doing the following:
1. Press Command+Option+Esc on the keyboard. The Force Quit window appears.
2. Find the application that is misbehaving. Its name is often followed by "(not
responding)" in the applications list.
3. Click that application, and then click Force Quit.
On a Windows Computer
Implement a force quit by doing the following:
1. Press Shift+Ctrl+Esc on the keyboard. The Windows Task Manager opens.
2. Find the application that is misbehaving.
3. Click that application, and then click the End Task button (in the bottom right).
If you have to force quit Unity while it's running, you will lose any work that
you've done in your scene since your last save. Because you must constantly
save C# scripts, they shouldn't be an issue, but you might have to redo unsaved
changes made to your scene. This is one of the reasons that I encourage you to
save your scenes as often as possible.
Enabling Debugging in Unity 2020
Prior to Unity version 2020, all code within the Unity Editor was always compiled in
Debug mode, allowing you to run the debugger at any time. However, with Unity's
recent moves toward efficiency and stability in the latest versions, all code now com-
piles in Release mode by default. Release mode code is faster and more efficient, but
you cannot attach a debugger to it. In Unity 2020.3, there is a new Debugging button in
the bottom-right of the Unity window that allows you to switch compilation to Debug
mode (shown in Figure 25.8).
Humble Bundle Pearson Game Design and Development Bundle — © Pearson. Do Not Distribute.

Figure 25.8 The Debugging button showing three states
To prepare Unity for debugging:
1. If your Unity editor is currently in release mode (the Debugging button is gray), click
the Debugging button (featured in Figure 25.8, "Release Mode"), which opens a
window explaining the different code compilation modes.
2. Click the Switch to debug mode button. The bug should now indicate it is in Debug
mode by changing to a yellow bug icon with an exclamation point (as shown in
Figure 25.8, "Debug Mode").
Now that your Unity Editor is in Debug mode, you can attach the Visual Studio
debugger to it.
Attaching the Debugger to Unity
For Visual Studio to be able to debug what's happening in Unity when it plays, you need
to attach it to the Unity process, which connects the debugger to the internals of Unity's
code execution. After you attach the Visual Studio debugger to Unity, it will be able to

In macOS, the process in Visual Studio is simpler than in Windows, but choosing the

for each of those). Sadly, you're just going to have to guess which is the right one. I usu-
ally just double-click the top one and hope for the best. (The Windows version of this
window does know which process is which, so I'm hoping that will come to macOS by
the time you read this chapter.)

If you are using Windows, and your Visual Studio is showing something other
than the Attach to Unity button shown in Figure 25.10a, you can try these steps
to repair it. This is not guaranteed to work, but it did fix the issue for me and some
others who tested it:
4
1. Close Visual Studio.
2. From the Unity menu, choose File > Build Settings….
3. In the Build Settings window, check the box next to Development Build and
close the Build Settings window.
4. From the Unity menu, choose Edit > Preferences….
5. Click External Tools on the left side of the Preferences window.
6. Set External Script Editor to Open by file extension and wait for Unity to think
about it.
7. Set External Script Editor to Visual Studio Community 20xx and wait for Unity
to think about it.
8. Click Regenerate project files.
9. Close the Preferences window.
10. Double-click a C# script in the Project pane to reopen Visual Studio.
If all went well, then when Visual Studio opens, the Attach to Unity button will
now be there.
